20:8.body: Deuteronomy's version says שמור, "keep". Rashi says God said זכור and שמור in one utterance, while Ibn Ezra says Moses kept the meaning, not the exact words, when he repeated it.

sources.quote: זָכוֹר וְשָׁמוֹר בְּדִבּוּר אֶחָד נֶאֶמְרוּ
sources.says: Rashi says "remember" and "keep" were said in a single utterance.

sources.quote: ועתה אדבר על זכור ושמור, דע כי הטעמים הם שמורים לא המלות
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the meanings are preserved, not the words.

20:11.headline: Did God "rest" on the seventh day, or stop?
20:11.body: Rashi says God, so to speak, wrote "rest" about Himself to teach people to rest. Maimonides says וינח here means God stopped, the way people stop speaking, or that He kept the world steady as it was.

sources.quote: כִּבְיָכוֹל הִכְתִּיב בְּעַצְמוֹ מְנוּחָה, לְלַמֵּד הֵימֶנּוּ קַל וָחֹמֶר לָאָדָם
sources.says: Rashi says God wrote rest about Himself to teach people all the more to rest.

sources.ref: Guide for the Perplexed, Part 1, Chapter 67
sources.quote: וכן נאמר על הפסקת הדיבור לשון ניחה
sources.says: Maimonides says the word for rest is also used for stopping speech.

sources.ref: Guide for the Perplexed, Part 1, Chapter 67
sources.quote: ולפי המשמעות הזו נאמר גם "וַיָּנַח בַּיּוֹם הַשְּׁבִיעִי"
sources.says: He says "and He rested on the seventh day" is said in that sense of stopping.

sources.ref: Guide for the Perplexed, Part 1, Chapter 67
sources.quote: ומשמעותו היא: ויִיצֵּב, או התמיד, את המציאות כפי שהיא כעת, ביום השביעי
sources.says: He offers another reading: on the seventh day God made the world stay as it now is.

20:13.headline: Not "do not kill" but "do not murder"
20:13.body: Hebrew has two verbs for killing. Rashbam says רצח always means killing without cause, while הרג can also be a lawful killing, so the command forbids murder.

sources.quote: כל רציחה - הריגה בחנם היא בכל מקום
sources.says: Rashbam says every use of רצח means killing for no reason.

sources.quote: אבל הריגה ומיתה יש בחנם כמו: ויהרגהו דקין. ויש בדין
sources.says: Rashbam says הרג can be unjust, like Cain's, or lawful.

20:13.headline: "Do not steal" here means do not kidnap
20:13.body: Rashi says this command is about stealing a person, since it sits beside murder and adultery, which carry the death penalty. Sforno agrees that is its main sense, but says it also covers stealing money and deceiving people.

sources.quote: בְּגוֹנֵב נְפָשׁוֹת הַכָּתוּב מְדַבֵּר
sources.says: Rashi says the verse speaks about kidnapping.

sources.quote: בִּכְלַל גְּנֵבָה גְּנֵבַת נְפָשׁוֹת וּגְנֵבַת מָמוֹן וּגְנֵבַת דַּעַת הַבְּרִיּוֹת
sources.says: Sforno says it includes stealing people, stealing money, and deceiving people.

20:14.headline: How can anyone be commanded not to want something?
20:14.body: Ibn Ezra asks how a person can stop wanting what is beautiful. He answers with a parable: a sensible villager does not long for a princess, because he knows she is out of reach, and so a wise person does not want what is not his.

sources.quote: אנשים רבים יתמהו על זאת המצוה, איך יהיה אדם שלא יחמוד דבר יפה בלבו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says many wonder how a person could not desire something beautiful.

sources.quote: דע כי איש כפרי שיש לו דעת נכונה, והוא ראה בת מלך שהיא יפה לא יחמוד אותה בלבו
sources.says: He says a sensible villager who sees a beautiful princess does not desire her.

20:15.headline: The people "saw" the sounds
20:15.body: Rashi says they saw what is normally only heard, which could happen nowhere else. Rabbeinu Bahya says "seeing" here means understanding, and Maimonides teaches that ראה is used for grasping with the mind as well as seeing with the eye.

sources.quote: רוֹאִין אֶת הַנִּשְׁמָע, שֶׁאִי אֶפְשָׁר לִרְאוֹת בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר
sources.says: Rashi says they saw what is heard, which is impossible anywhere else.

sources.quote: ראיה זו ענין השגה
sources.says: Rabbeinu Bahya says this seeing means understanding.

sources.ref: Guide for the Perplexed, Part 1, Chapter 4
sources.quote: משמשים במובן של ראיית העין, ושלושתם הושאלו להשגת השכל
sources.says: Maimonides says the words for seeing mean sight with the eye and are also borrowed for understanding.

20:17.headline: God came to "test" you, or to "raise you up"?
20:17.body: נסות usually means "to test", and Ibn Ezra reads it that way. Rashi reads it from נס, a banner raised high: God came to lift Israel's name among the nations.

sources.quote: לְשׁוֹן הֲרָמָה וּגְדֻלָּה, כְּמוֹ הָרִימוּ נֵס
sources.says: Rashi says נסות means raising up and greatness, like "raise a banner".

sources.quote: לְגַדֵּל אֶתְכֶם בָּעוֹלָם, שֶׁיֵּצֵא לָכֶם שֵׁם בָּאֻמּוֹת
sources.says: Rashi says God came to make Israel great, so that its name would go out among the nations.

sources.quote: וטעם נסות אתכם. כמו ולמען נסותך להטיבך באחריתך
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says נסות means testing, as in "to test you, to do you good in the end".

20:18.headline: Was the ערפל thick darkness, or blinding light?
20:18.body: Rashi says ערפל is the thickest cloud, the last of three layers around God. Rabbeinu Bahya splits the word into ערוי אפל, "darkness emptied out", and says it was a light so strong that no one could look into it.

sources.quote: לִפְנִים מִשָּׁלֹשׁ מְחִצּוֹת: חֹשֶׁךְ, עָנָן, וַעֲרָפֶל
sources.says: Rashi says Moses went inside three barriers: darkness, cloud, and ערפל.

sources.quote: והנכון לפרש כי ערפל הוא אור צח בהיר ובאור המלה ערפל ערוי אפל כלומר שהאופל מעורה ונעדר משם
sources.says: Rabbeinu Bahya says ערפל is a pure bright light, and the word means darkness emptied out and gone.

21:1.headline: The 'and' that ties these civil laws to Sinai
21:1.body: The chapter opens with 'and these', ואלה. Rashi says the 'and' joins these laws to the Ten Commandments before them: as those came from Sinai, so did these.

sources.quote: ואלה מוסיף על הראשונים, מה הראשונים מסיני, אף אלו מסיני
sources.says: Rashi says 'and these' adds to what came before: as the earlier laws were from Sinai, so are these.

21:1.headline: Laws set out like a laid table, or like a drug
21:1.body: Rashi says Moses must set the laws before the people like a table laid and ready to eat, with their reasons explained. Rabbeinu Bahya hears סם, a drug, in תשים: for a just judge the law is a medicine of life, for an unjust one a poison.

sources.quote: כשלחן הערוך ומוכן לאכל לפני האדם
sources.says: Rashi says the laws must be set out like a table laid and ready for a person to eat.

sources.quote: שלכך הזכיר לשון תשים מלשון סם
sources.says: Bahya says the Torah uses תשים because it sounds like סם, a drug.

sources.quote: שאם הדיין שופט בצדק הוא לו סם חיים
sources.says: Bahya says that if the judge rules justly, the law is a medicine of life for him.

21:2.headline: A Hebrew servant, or a Hebrew's servant?
21:2.body: עבד עברי could mean a servant who is a Hebrew, or a servant owned by a Hebrew. Rashi uses the verse 'your brother the Hebrew' to show it means a fellow Hebrew who is himself the servant.

sources.quote: עבד שהוא עברי; או אינו אלא עבדו של עברי
sources.says: Rashi asks whether it means a servant who is a Hebrew, or the servant of a Hebrew.

sources.quote: ת"ל כי ימכר לך אחיך העברי (דברים ט"ו), לא אמרתי אלא באחיך
sources.says: Rashi answers from Deuteronomy that the law speaks of your brother.

21:3.headline: He came in 'with his wing': alone, with only his clothes
21:3.body: Onkelos translates בגפו as 'alone', meaning unmarried. Rashi hears כנף, the edge of a garment: he came in with nothing but the clothes he wore, while some in Ibn Ezra read גוף, his body alone.

sources.quote: אם בלחודוהי ייעול
sources.says: Onkelos translates: if he comes in alone.

sources.quote: ולשון בגפו – בכנפו, שלא בא אלא כמות שהוא, יחידי, בתוך לבושו
sources.says: Rashi says בגפו means with his wing: he came just as he was, alone, inside his clothing.

sources.quote: י"א בגפו כמו בגופו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra reports that some read בגפו as 'with his body'.

21:6.headline: Brought 'to God', which here means to the judges
21:6.body: Rashi and Onkelos read האלהים here as the court. Ramban gives Ibn Ezra's reason, that judges carry out God's justice, and adds that it hints God himself stands with the judges.

sources.quote: אל האלהים. לבית דין
sources.says: Rashi says 'to God' means to the court.

sources.quote: ויקרבנה רבונה לקדם דיניא
sources.says: Onkelos translates: his master brings him before the judges.

sources.quote: כי נקראו השופטים אלהים בעבור שהם מקימי משפטי האלהים בארץ
sources.says: Ramban cites Ibn Ezra that judges are called אלהים because they carry out God's laws on earth.

sources.quote: לרמז כי האלהים יהיה עמהם בדבר המשפט
sources.says: Ramban says it hints that God will be with them in judgment.

21:6.headline: Why pierce the ear?
21:6.body: Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai says this ear heard at Sinai 'do not steal' and 'the children of Israel are My servants', yet the man stole or chose a human master. Rabbi Shimon adds that it is done at the door, which witnessed the Exodus.

sources.quote: אזן זאת ששמעה על הר סיני לא תגנב, והלך וגנב, תרצע
sources.says: Rashi quotes Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai: the ear that heard 'do not steal' at Sinai, and went and stole, should be pierced.

sources.quote: עבדי הם ולא עבדים לעבדים
sources.says: Rashi says Israel are God's servants, not servants of servants.

sources.quote: דלת ומזוזה שהיו עדים במצרים
sources.says: Rashi quotes Rabbi Shimon: the door and doorpost were witnesses in Egypt.

21:6.headline: The awl whose letters add up to 400 years
21:6.body: The letters of מרצע, awl, add up to 400. Chizkuni cites a midrash: God cut short the 400 years of slavery decreed on Israel, so a man who chooses to stay a servant is pierced with a tool whose number is 400.

sources.quote: אני גזרתי על ישראל שעבוד של ארבע מאות שנה
sources.says: Chizkuni quotes a midrash: God says, I decreed 400 years of servitude on Israel.

sources.quote: והלך זה ושעבד את עצמו ירצע בכלי שהוא עולה בגימטריא
sources.says: Chizkuni says this man who enslaved himself is pierced with a tool whose number value is 400, the מרצע.

21:6.headline: A servant 'forever', or only until the Jubilee?
21:6.body: Rashi, with the sages, says לעלם here means until the Jubilee year, and Ibn Ezra says עולם can mean a set span of time. Rashbam says the plain sense is all his life.

sources.quote: ועבדו לעלם. עד היובל
sources.says: Rashi says 'forever' means until the Jubilee.

sources.quote: כי מלת לעולם בלשון הקדש הוא זמן
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says לעולם in Hebrew means a span of time.

sources.quote: לפי הפשט: כל ימי חייו
sources.says: Rashbam says by the plain meaning it is all the days of his life.

21:8.headline: Betraying her, or spreading his cloak over her?
21:8.body: בבגדו can come from בגידה, betrayal, or from בגד, a garment. Rabbi Eliezer reads betrayal, but Rabbi Akiva reads garment: once he spread his cloak over her in betrothal, he may not sell her.

sources.quote: זה מבין מלשון בגידה וזה מבין מלשון בגד
sources.says: Bahya says one sage reads the word as betrayal and the other as garment.

sources.quote: כיון שפרש טליתו עליה שוב אינו רשאי למכרה
sources.says: Bahya gives Rabbi Akiva's reading: once he spread his cloak over her, he may no longer sell her.

21:10.headline: A wife's right: her time together with him, or her home?
21:10.body: ענתה appears only here. Rashi reads it as a wife's right to marital relations, and Ibn Ezra ties it to עת, the time of love, while Rashbam reads it as her home, from מעון, a dwelling.

sources.quote: ענתה. תשמיש
sources.says: Rashi says it means marital relations.

sources.quote: ופי' ועונתה על המשכב שהוא עת דודים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it refers to lying together, the time of love.

sources.quote: ועונתה - בית דירה. לפי הפשט ל' מעון
sources.says: Rashbam says it means a house to live in, from מעון, by the plain sense.

21:13.headline: God arranges the accident: two killers meet at one inn
21:13.body: Rashi reads אנה as 'God brought it about', and tells how: one man killed on purpose and another by accident, and neither was punished for lack of witnesses. God brings them to one inn, where the accidental killer falls from a ladder onto the murderer before witnesses.

sources.quote: והאלהים אנה לידו. זמן לידו
sources.says: Rashi says it means God made it happen to him.

sources.quote: והקב"ה מזמנן לפנדק אחד
sources.says: Rashi says God brings the two of them to one inn.

sources.quote: נמצא זה שהרג בשוגג גולה, וזה שהרג במזיד נהרג
sources.says: Rashi says in the end the accidental killer goes into exile and the deliberate killer is put to death.

21:18.headline: A fist, or a lump of stone?
21:18.body: Ramban, with the sages, reads אגרף as a fist. Onkelos and Rashbam read it as a kind of stone or brick, and Chizkuni asks why the verse would need to say 'he did not die' about a punch.

sources.quote: אגרוף הוא היד שיקבצו האצבעות לתוך הכף להכות בה
sources.says: Ramban says an אגרוף is the hand with the fingers closed into the palm to strike.

sources.quote: לפי הפשט: כתרגומו, מין אבן או לבנה
sources.says: Rashbam says by the plain sense, as Onkelos translates, it is a kind of stone or brick.

sources.quote: וכי בשביל מכת יד היה לו למות
sources.says: Chizkuni asks whether a blow of the hand would ever be expected to kill.

21:19.headline: Walking 'on his staff': healthy again, or on a real cane?
21:19.body: Rashi, from the Mekhilta, reads 'on his staff' as on his own strength, healthy again. Ramban says it is a real walking stick: once the injured man walks outside with a cane, the one who hit him is cleared.

sources.quote: על משענתו. על בריו וכחו
sources.says: Rashi says 'on his staff' means in his health and strength.

sources.quote: ולפי דעתי כי משענתו כפשוטו
sources.says: Ramban says in his view משענתו means a staff, as it plainly reads.

21:19.headline: Permission for doctors to heal
21:19.body: From 'he shall surely heal' the sages learned that doctors are allowed to heal and need not leave it all to God. Ibn Ezra and Rabbeinu Bahya limit this to wounds on the outside of the body.

sources.quote: ורפא ירפא מכאן שנתנה רשות לרופא לרפאות
sources.says: Bahya quotes the sages: from here, permission was given to the doctor to heal.

sources.quote: לאות שנתן רשות לרופאים לרפא המכות והפצעים שיראו בחוץ
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it shows doctors were permitted to heal the wounds seen on the outside.

21:23.headline: 'A life for a life': death, or payment?
21:23.body: If the woman dies, the verse says 'a life for a life'. Rashi reports that the sages disagree: some say the striker really dies, others say he pays money, since he meant to hit someone else.

sources.quote: יש אומרים נפש ממש, ויש אומרים ממון אבל לא נפש ממש
sources.says: Rashi says some sages read it as a real life, and others as money, not a real life.

21:24.headline: 'An eye for an eye' means paying for the eye
21:24.body: The sages read the verse as paying the value of the eye, not taking one. Sforno says strict justice would be measure for measure, but the tradition set money, since we might misjudge and do more harm than was done.

sources.quote: סמא עין חברו נותן לו דמי עינו
sources.says: Rashi says one who blinds his friend's eye pays him the worth of the eye.

sources.quote: ולא נטילת אבר ממש
sources.says: Rashi says it does not mean actually taking a limb.

sources.quote: ובאה הקבלה שישלם ממון
sources.says: Sforno says the tradition came that he pays money.

sources.quote: מפני חסרון השערתנו, פן נסכל ונוסיף על המדה
sources.says: Sforno says this is because our judgment is limited, and we might go beyond the measure.

21:28.headline: An ox 'gores' a person but only 'strikes' an ox
21:28.body: When an ox kills a person the verse says יגח, gores; when it kills an ox it says יגף, strikes. Rabbeinu Bahya cites the Talmud: a person has a guiding fortune, so an ox must gore on purpose to kill him, while an animal can die from a chance blow.

sources.quote: הזכיר באדם לשון נגיחה אבל בבהמה בשור שהמית שור הזכיר נגיפה
sources.says: Bahya notes the verse uses goring for a person but striking for an ox that kills an ox.

sources.quote: אדם דאית ליה מזלא הזכיר בו נגיחה
sources.says: Bahya says a person has a guiding fortune, so goring is said of him.

21:29.headline: Is the ox's owner really put to death?
21:29.body: Rashi says 'shall be put to death' here means death at the hands of Heaven, not by a court. Chizkuni says that by the plain sense he truly deserves death, since he knew his ox gored.

sources.quote: וגם בעליו יומת. בידי שמים
sources.says: Rashi says the owner's death is at the hands of Heaven.

sources.quote: על רציחתו אתה הורגו ואי אתה הורגו על רציחת שורו
sources.says: Rashi says a court executes a man for his own killing, not for his ox's.

sources.quote: לפי הפשט דין מיתה עליו שהרי יודע היה שהיה שורו נגחן
sources.says: Chizkuni says by the plain sense he is liable to die, since he knew his ox gored.

21:35.headline: An ox has no friends, says Ibn Ezra
21:35.body: Ben Zuta read רעהו as the ox's own fellow. Ibn Ezra answers that it means the owner's neighbor, and jokes that the only one who counts an ox as a friend is Ben Zuta himself.

sources.quote: אמר בן זוטא כי רעהו תואר לשור
sources.says: Ibn Ezra reports Ben Zuta's view that רעהו describes the ox.

sources.quote: ואין לשור ריע רק בן זוטא לבדו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says an ox has no friend except Ben Zuta himself.

21:37.headline: Five oxen but only four sheep: why?
21:37.body: Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai says the thief who carried a sheep on his shoulders was already shamed, so he pays less. Rabbi Meir says stealing an ox also took it away from its work.

sources.quote: חס המקום על כבודן של בריות
sources.says: Rashi quotes Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai: God cares for people's dignity.

sources.quote: שה שנושאו על כתפו, משלם ארבעה הואיל ונתבזה בו
sources.says: Rashi says for a sheep, carried on his shoulder, he pays four, since he was shamed by it.

sources.quote: שור שבטלו ממלאכתו חמשה
sources.says: Rashi quotes Rabbi Meir: for an ox, taken from its work, he pays five.

22:1.headline: 'He has no blood': killing a night burglar is not murder
22:1.body: Rashi says אין לו דמים, 'he has no blood', means killing a burglar at night is not murder: he counts as dead already. Ibn Ezra says it means the killer bears no bloodguilt, and he rejects reading דמים as 'life'.

sources.quote: אין לו דמים. אֵין זוֹ רְצִיחָה, הֲרֵי הוּא כְמֵת מֵעִקָּרוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says this is not murder; the burglar is as if dead from the start.

sources.quote: אין על הורגו שפיכות דמים, ויש לתמוה מן המפרשים דמים חיים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the one who kills him has no bloodguilt, and he wonders at those who explain דמים as 'life'.

22:2.headline: 'If the sun rose on him': daylight, or clear as day?
22:2.body: Rashbam reads it plainly: the thief came by day. Rashi says it is a figure of speech, meaning it is clear as the sun that the thief means no harm, and Onkelos reads it as 'if witnesses saw him'.

sources.quote: אם זרחה השמש - שהיה גונב ביום
sources.says: Rashbam says it means he was stealing by day.

sources.quote: אֵין זֶה אֶלָּא כְמִין מָשָׁל: אִם בָּרוּר לְךָ הַדָּבָר שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ שָׁלוֹם עִמְּךָ, כַּשֶּׁמֶשׁ הַזֶּה שֶׁהוּא שָׁלוֹם בָּעוֹלָם
sources.says: Rashi says it is only a kind of parable: if it is clear to you that he is at peace with you, as the sun brings peace to the world.

sources.quote: וְאֻנְקְלוֹס שֶׁתִּרְגֵּם אִם עֵינָא דְּסַהֲדַיָּא נְפָלַת עֲלוֹהִי, לָקַח לוֹ שִׁטָּה אַחֶרֶת
sources.says: Rashi notes that Onkelos translated 'if the eye of witnesses fell on him', taking a different approach.

22:4.headline: One root for livestock and for eating a field bare
22:4.body: Rashi says יבער, בעירה and ובער all come from בעיר, livestock: a man lets his animals graze in another's field. Chizkuni hears 'destroy' in it: the animals wipe the field clean of its crop.

sources.quote: כי יבער, את בעירה ובער. כֻּלָּם לְשׁוֹן בְּהֵמָה, כְּמוֹ אֲנַחְנוּ וּבְעִירֵנוּ
sources.says: Rashi says all three words mean animals, as in 'we and our cattle' (Numbers 20).

sources.quote: כי יבער איש שדה או כרם לשון ביעור וכליון
sources.says: Chizkuni says יבער means clearing out and destroying.

22:5.headline: The same word twice: grazing animals, then spreading fire
22:5.body: In verse 4 the root בער meant animals grazing. Here המבער is the one who lit a fire, and Ibn Ezra says using one word in two senses side by side is a mark of elegant Hebrew, like Samson's 'with a donkey's jaw, heap upon heaps'.

sources.quote: וטעם המבעיר אינו כמו יבער איש (פ' ד) אעפ"י שהם מבנין אחד, כי מלת אש תורה עליו, וזאת הדרך צחות בלשון הקדש לאמר מלה שוה, והיא משני טעמים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says המבעיר is not like יבער in verse 4, though they share a form, since the word 'fire' shows its sense; saying one word with two meanings is elegance in the holy tongue.

sources.quote: כמו בלחי החמור חמור חמורתים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra compares Samson's line 'with the jaw of a donkey, a heap, two heaps'.

22:12.headline: Bring a witness, or bring the torn remains as proof?
22:12.body: Rashi reads עד as 'witness': the shepherd brings people who saw the beast attack. Ibn Ezra says he brings part of the torn animal as evidence, like the shepherd in Amos who saves 'two legs or a piece of an ear' from the lion.

sources.quote: יביאהו עד. יָבִיא עֵדִים שֶׁנִּטְרְפָה בְאֹנֶס וּפָטוּר
sources.says: Rashi says he brings witnesses that the animal was torn by force he could not stop, and he is exempt.

sources.quote: יביא קצת הנטרף להיות לו לעד על דרך שכתוב כאשר יציל הרועה מפי הארי שתי כרעים או בדל אזן
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says he brings part of the torn animal as his evidence, as in 'as the shepherd rescues from the lion's mouth two legs or a piece of an ear' (Amos 3:12).

22:20.headline: The stranger is named like a lone berry on a branch
22:20.body: Rashi says a גר is anyone not born in the land who came from elsewhere to live there. Bahya hears in the word a גרגיר, a single berry left alone at the top of a branch, which is why the Torah guards the stranger so often.

sources.quote: כָּל לְשׁוֹן גֵּר אָדָם שֶׁלֹּא נוֹלַד בְּאוֹתָהּ מְדִינָה, אֶלָּא בָּא מִמְּדִינָה אַחֶרֶת לָגוּר שָׁם
sources.says: Rashi says a גר is a person not born in that country, who came from another country to live there.

sources.quote: בכמה מקומות כתוב בתורה והזהיר הקב"ה על הגר לפי שהגר הוא מוצא עצמו יחידי בארץ נכריה ולכך נקרא גר מלשון גרגיר הנמצא יחידי בראש ענף האילן
sources.says: Bahya says the Torah warns about the stranger in many places because he finds himself alone in a foreign land, and he is called גר like a lone berry at the top of a branch.

22:20.headline: 'You were strangers': two reasons not to wrong the stranger
22:20.body: Rashi says if you taunt a stranger he can answer that you too come from strangers, so do not mock a flaw you share. Ramban reads it differently: you know from Egypt that God sees the oppressed stranger and punishes the oppressor.

sources.quote: אִם הוֹנִיתוֹ, אַף הוּא יָכוֹל לְהוֹנוֹתְךָ וְלוֹמַר לְךָ, אַף אַתָּה מִגֵּרִים בָּאתָ, "מוּם שֶׁבְּךָ אַל תֹּאמַר לַחֲבֵרְךָ
sources.says: Rashi says if you wrong him with words, he can wrong you back: you too came from strangers; do not point out in your fellow a flaw you have yourself.

sources.quote: כִּי אַתָּה יָדַעְתָּ שֶׁהֱיִיתֶם גֵּרִים בְּאֶרֶץ מִצְרַיִם וְרָאִיתִי אֶת הַלַּחַץ אֲשֶׁר מִצְרַיִם לֹחֲצִים אֶתְכֶם וְעָשִׂיתִי בָּהֶם נְקָמָה
sources.says: Ramban says the reason is: you know you were strangers in Egypt, and God saw how Egypt oppressed you and took revenge on them.

22:21.headline: Why 'do not afflict' is said to everyone at once
22:21.body: Unlike the laws around it, לא תענון is in the plural. Ibn Ezra and Chizkuni say anyone who sees a widow or orphan mistreated and stays silent counts as an abuser too.

sources.quote: ואחר שאמר לא תענון לשון רבים אמר אם תענה, כי כל רואה אדם שהוא מענה יתום ואלמנה ולא יעזרם, גם הוא יחשב מענה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says 'you shall not afflict' is plural because anyone who sees a person afflict an orphan or widow and does not help them is also counted as afflicting.

sources.quote: מצוה זו כתובה בלשון רבים מה שאין כן בכל הדינין הכתובים בפרשה זו לפי שכולם פושעים בם אפילו אותם שאינם מקניטים שהרי רואים הם עלבונם ושותקים
sources.says: Chizkuni says this law alone in the section is in the plural, because everyone sins in it, even those who do not taunt, since they see the insult and keep silent.

22:24.headline: 'If you lend' really means 'when you lend'
22:24.body: אם usually means 'if', as if the choice were yours. Rashi quotes Rabbi Yishmael: every אם in the Torah is optional except three, and this is one of them.

sources.quote: רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל אוֹמֵר כָּל אִם וְאִם שֶׁבַּתּוֹרָה רְשׁוּת חוּץ מִשְּׁלֹשָׁה, וְזֶה אֶחָד מֵהֶן
sources.says: Rashi quotes Rabbi Yishmael: every 'if' in the Torah is optional except three, and this is one of them.

22:24.headline: 'The poor one with you': picture yourself in his place
22:24.body: The verse calls the poor person עמך, 'with you'. Rashi reads it as advice to the lender: look at yourself as if you were the poor one.

sources.quote: את העני עמך. הֱוֵי מִסְתַּכֵּל בְּעַצְמְךָ כְּאִלּוּ אַתָּה עָנִי
sources.says: Rashi says: look at yourself as if you were poor.

22:24.headline: Interest is called a 'bite', like a snake's
22:24.body: נשך, interest, comes from the word for biting. Rashi says it is like a snakebite: a small wound you hardly feel that then swells up to your head, just as interest grows until it eats up a great deal of money.

sources.quote: נשך. רִבִּית, שֶׁהוּא כִנְשִׁיכַת נָחָשׁ שֶׁנוֹשֵׁךְ חַבּוּרָה קְטַנָּה בְּרַגְלוֹ וְאֵינוֹ מַרְגִּישׁ, וּפִתְאֹם הוּא מְבַטְבֵּט וְנוֹפֵחַ עַד קָדְקֳדוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says interest is like a snake's bite: a small wound on the foot that is not felt, then suddenly it swells up to the top of the head.

sources.quote: כָּךְ רִבִּית אֵינוֹ מַרְגִּישׁ וְאֵינוֹ נִכָּר עַד שֶׁהָרִבִּית עוֹלָה וּמְחַסְּרוֹ מָמוֹן הַרְבֵּה
sources.says: Rashi says interest too is not felt or noticed until it mounts up and costs the borrower a great deal of money.

22:25.headline: Take the pledge and give it back, as God returns your soul
22:25.body: The verb is doubled, חבל תחבל. Rashi says God tells the lender: your soul comes up to Me every night owing Me and I give it back, so you too take and return, take and return.

sources.quote: אָמַר הַקָּבָּ"ה כַּמָּה אַתָּה חַיָּב לִי, וַהֲרֵי נַפְשְׁךָ עוֹלָה אֶצְלִי כָּל אֶמֶשׁ וָאֶמֶשׁ וְנוֹתֶנֶת דִּין וּמִתְחַיֶּבֶת לְפָנַי וַאֲנִי מַחֲזִירָהּ לְךָ, אַף אַתָּה טֹל וְהָשֵׁב טֹל וְהָשֵׁב
sources.says: Rashi says God tells the lender: how much you owe Me, yet your soul rises to Me every night, is judged and found guilty, and I return it to you; so you too take and return, take and return.

22:27.headline: Do not curse אלהים: God, or the judge?
22:27.body: Rashi says the verse warns at once against cursing God and against cursing a judge. Ibn Ezra reads אלהים here as the judges, and Ramban says the word covers both God and the judge who sits in God's place on earth.

sources.quote: הֲרֵי זוֹ אַזְהָרָה לְבִרְכַּת הַשֵּׁם וְאַזְהָרָה לְקִלְלַת דַּיָּן
sources.says: Rashi says this is a warning against cursing God's name and a warning against cursing a judge.

sources.quote: אלהים לא תקלל. הם הדיינים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says אלהים here are the judges.

sources.quote: כִּי יִכָּנֵס בִּכְלַל "אֱלֹהִים" הַשֵּׁם הַנִּכְבָּד וְהַשּׁוֹפֵט אֲשֶׁר יֵשֵׁב מוֹשַׁב אֱלֹהִים בָּאָרֶץ
sources.says: Ramban says the word אלהים includes both God's honored name and the judge who sits in God's seat on earth.

22:28.headline: Rashi admits he does not know why it is called 'tear'
22:28.body: דמע means a tear. Rashi says it is the priests' portion but admits he does not know what the word means, while Bahya says it is the oil pressed from olives, which comes out in drops like a tear from the eye.

sources.quote: ודמעך. הַתְּרוּמָה – וְאֵינִי יוֹדֵעַ מַהוּ לְשׁוֹן דֶּמַע
sources.says: Rashi says it is the terumah, the priests' portion, and he does not know what the word דמע means.

sources.quote: ומלת ודמעך שם המשקה היוצא מן הזיתים ע"י סחיטה וכתישה כדמעה היוצאה מן העין לכך קרוי דמעך
sources.says: Bahya says it is the liquid that comes from olives by squeezing and crushing, like a tear from the eye, and so it is called דמע.

22:30.headline: The dog gets the torn meat as pay for staying silent
22:30.body: Rashi says the Torah names the dog to teach that God never withholds any creature's reward. The dogs did not bark when Israel left Egypt, so God said: give them their pay.

sources.quote: וְלִמֶּדְךָ הַכָּתוּב שֶׁאֵין הַקָּבָּ"ה מְקַפֵּחַ שְׂכַר כָּל בְּרִיָּה, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר וּלְכָל בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל לֹא יֶחֱרַץ כֶּלֶב לְשֹׁנוֹ (שמות י"א), אָמַר הַקָּבָּ"ה תְּנוּ לוֹ שְׂכָרוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says the verse teaches that God does not hold back the reward of any creature, as it says no dog barked at the Israelites (Exodus 11), so God said: give it its reward.

23:2.headline: A dispute, or the great one of the court?
23:2.body: The word is written רב with no yod, and Ibn Ezra reads it as ריב, a dispute. The sages read it as רַב, the great one of the court, and Rashi records this but says it does not fit the plain words.

sources.quote: לא תענה על רב – על רב, שאין חולקין על מפלא שבבית דין
sources.says: Rashi brings the sages' reading: do not disagree with the most distinguished judge of the court.

sources.quote: יש במקרא זה מדרשי חכמי ישראל, אבל אין לשון המקרא מישב בהן על אפניו
sources.says: Rashi says the sages read this verse in several ways, but the language of the verse does not sit well with them.

sources.quote: לא תענה על ריב. מצוה על כל ישראל
sources.says: Ibn Ezra reads the word as ריב, a dispute, and says the command is for all Israel.

23:8.headline: Not the words of the righteous, but words that are right
23:8.body: דברי צדיקים sounds like 'the words of righteous people', but Rashi says it means words that are just: true rulings. Ibn Ezra says it means people in the right in a case, not people who keep the commandments.

sources.quote: דברי צדיקים. דברים המצדקים, משפטי אמת
sources.says: Rashi says it means words that are just: true rulings.

sources.quote: וטעם צדיקים בדין, לא צדיקים במצות
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means those in the right in a case, not those righteous in keeping the commandments.

23:14.headline: Three 'feet' a year: times, and journeys on foot
23:14.body: רגלים literally means feet, but Rashi says here it means times, as when Balaam's donkey was struck 'three רגלים'. Ibn Ezra adds that most pilgrims came on foot, and a midrash in Bahya says they should go up only walking.

sources.quote: רגלים. פעמים; וכן כי הכיתני זה שלש רגלים
sources.says: Rashi says it means times, as in Balaam's donkey saying 'you have struck me three times'.

sources.quote: רגלים. מגזרת רגל כי רובם רגלים הם
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word comes from foot, because most of the pilgrims came on foot.

sources.quote: אזהרה לישראל שלא יעלו אלא ברגליהם
sources.says: Bahya cites a midrash that Israel is told to go up only on foot.

23:15.headline: The spring month is named for the first ripe grain
23:15.body: Passover falls in חדש האביב. Rashi says אביב comes from אב, father, meaning first: it is the month when the grain fills out and ripens first.

sources.quote: אביב לשון אב, בכור וראשון לבשל פרות
sources.says: Rashi says אביב comes from אב, meaning the firstborn, the first to ripen fruit.

23:19.headline: Not only a young goat, but any young animal
23:19.body: גדי usually means a young goat. Rashi notes that the Torah often adds 'of the goats' after it, which shows the word alone means any tender young animal, calf and lamb included.

sources.quote: שאין גדי אלא לשון ולד רך
sources.says: Rashi says גדי simply means a tender young animal.

sources.quote: ללמדך שכל מקום שנאמר גדי סתם אף עגל וכבש במשמע
sources.says: Rashi says that wherever גדי stands alone, a calf and a lamb are included.

23:20.headline: A place prepared for you, or a place facing Mine
23:20.body: Plainly the angel leads Israel to the place God set aside for them. Rashi also brings a midrash: God's own place above already faces it, so the Temple in heaven stands opposite the one on earth.

sources.quote: אשר זמנתי לתת לכם, זהו פשוטו
sources.says: Rashi says the plain meaning is the place God set aside to give them.

sources.quote: שבית המקדש של מעלה מכון כנגד של מטה
sources.says: Rashi brings the midrash that the Temple above is set directly opposite the Temple below.

23:21.headline: An angel who carries God's own name
23:21.body: Rashi says 'My name is in him' explains the start of the verse: beware of the angel, because God's name is bound up in him. The sages said this is Metatron, whose name equals Shaddai in number value.

sources.quote: השמר מפניו כי שמי משתף בו
sources.says: Rashi says the verse means: beware of him, because My name is joined with him.

sources.quote: ורבותינו אמרו זה מטטרון ששמו כשם רבו, מטטרון בגימטריא שדי
sources.says: Rashi says the sages identified him as Metatron, whose name is like his Master's, and whose letters add up to Shaddai.

23:27.headline: 'I will throw them into panic', not 'I will kill them'
23:27.body: והמתי could be read 'I will kill', but Rashi and Rashbam say it comes from המם, to throw into confusion, as Onkelos translates. Rashbam notes that 'I will kill' would be said differently.

sources.quote: והמתי. כמו והממתי, ותרגומו ואשגש
sources.says: Rashi says it is like 'I will confound', and Onkelos translates 'I will confuse'.

sources.quote: והמתי - והממתי מהומת קולי
sources.says: Rashbam says it means I will throw them into panic with My voice.

sources.quote: אבל לשון מיתה יאמר והמתי
sources.says: Rashbam says the word for killing would be pronounced differently.

23:28.headline: A stinging insect, or a disease?
23:28.body: Rashi says הצרעה is a flying insect that struck the enemy in the eyes and poisoned them. Ibn Ezra reads it from צרעת, a skin disease: a blow to the body that weakens it.

sources.quote: הצרעה. מין שרץ העוף, והיתה מכה אותם בעיניהם ומטילה בהם ארס
sources.says: Rashi says it is a flying insect that struck them in the eyes and injected poison.

sources.quote: ושלחתי את הצרעה. מכה בגוף מגזרת צרעת
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it is a bodily plague, from the same root as צרעת.

24:10.headline: Under God's feet, "sapphire brickwork": a memory of the slaves' bricks
24:10.body: Under God's feet was something like לבנת הספיר. Rashi reads לבנת as brickwork: God kept it before Him to remember Israel making bricks in Egypt. Rashbam reads it as whiteness. Maimonides says it means clearness, like clear crystal.

sources.quote: לִזְכֹּר צָרָתָן שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁהָיוּ מְשֻׁעְבָּדִים בְּמַעֲשֵׂה לְבֵנִים
sources.says: Rashi says it was before God during the slavery, to remember Israel's pain as they were forced to make bricks.

sources.quote: לבנת - לובן
sources.says: Rashbam says לבנת means whiteness.

sources.quote: ואילו "לבנת הספיר" הוא ביטוי לשקיפות, לא לצבע הלבן
sources.says: Maimonides says "the whiteness of sapphire" means transparency, not the color white.

24:10.headline: "Like the bone of the sky": here עצם means the look of it
24:10.body: עצם usually means a bone, or the thing itself. Here it is "like the עצם of the heavens". Rashi and Rashbam say it means appearance, and Rashbam points to Lamentations, "their appearance was redder than coral".

sources.quote: כְּתַרְגּוּמוֹ, לְשׁוֹן מַרְאֶה
sources.says: Rashi says, following the Targum, that it means appearance.

sources.quote: וכעצם - מראה כמו: [איכה ד] אדמו עצם מפנינים
sources.says: Rashbam says it means appearance, as in Lamentations 4, "they were redder in appearance than coral".

24:11.headline: The "nobles" of Israel: those on whom God's spirit was set
24:11.body: אצילי, "the nobles", is a rare word. Rashi says it means the great ones. Ramban and Rabbeinu Bahya tie it to the verb for setting spirit upon someone: they were called this because God's spirit was set upon them.

sources.quote: אצילי. לְשׁוֹן גְּדוֹלִים
sources.says: Rashi says אצילי means great ones, as in "from its nobles I called you".

sources.quote: וּקְרָאָם כֵּן כִּי נֶאֱצַל עֲלֵיהֶם רוּחַ אֱלֹהִים
sources.says: Ramban says they were called this because the spirit of God was set upon them.

sources.quote: נקראו אצילי מלשון אצילות כלומר שנאצל עליהם רוח נבואה
sources.says: Rabbeinu Bahya says they were called this because a spirit of prophecy was set upon them.

24:16.headline: The cloud "covered it", or covered him? Mountain or Moses
24:16.body: The verse says the cloud ויכסהו, "covered it/him", for six days. Rashi brings both readings: the cloud covered the mountain, or it covered Moses. Ibn Ezra says it covered Moses, so no one could see him.

sources.quote: ויכסהו הענן. לָהָר
sources.says: Rashi says the cloud covered the mountain.

sources.quote: ויכסהו הענן לְמֹשֶׁה ששת ימים לְאַחַר עֲשֶׂרֶת הַדִּבְּרוֹת
sources.says: Rashi brings another view: the cloud covered Moses for six days after the Ten Commandments.

sources.quote: ויכסהו הענן. את משה ואדם לא ראהו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the cloud covered Moses, and no person saw him.

25:3.headline: Gold comes first: a sign the golden calf was forgiven
25:3.body: The list of gifts opens with gold. Rabbeinu Bahya says this hints that the sin of the golden calf had already been forgiven. He also cites a midrash that gold, silver and copper stand for the empires of Babylon, Media and Greece.

sources.quote: ומה שהזכיר בכאן זהב בראש התרומה לרמוז שכבר נמחל להם עון העגל שהיה של זהב
sources.says: Rabbeinu Bahya says gold is listed first to hint that the sin of the golden calf had been forgiven.

sources.quote: ובמדרש זהב וכסף ונחשת, זהב כנגד מלכות בבל
sources.says: Rabbeinu Bahya cites a midrash that the gold stands for the kingdom of Babylon.

25:4.headline: תכלת, the blue dye, heard as תכלית, the end of all colors
25:4.body: Rashi says תכלת is wool dyed with the blood of a sea creature, the חלזון. Ibn Ezra reports that Yefet thought it was nearly black, because it is the תכלית, the end point, of all colors. Ibn Ezra himself relies on the sages, who called its color ירוק.

sources.quote: צמר צבוע בדם חלזון וצבעו ירק
sources.says: Rashi says it is wool dyed with the blood of the חלזון, and its color is ירוק.

sources.quote: אמר יפת שהוא כדמות שחרות, כי הוא תכלית כל הצבעים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra reports Yefet's view that it was close to black, since it is the end point of all colors.

sources.quote: ואנו נסמוך על רז"ל שאמרו שהוא ירוק
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says he relies on the sages, who said it is ירוק.

25:4.headline: 'Worm' scarlet: red wool, not silk
25:4.body: תולעת means worm. Rashbam says here it is the name for wool dyed red, and שני is the dye. Ibn Ezra reports that because of the word 'worm', many thought it was silk. Rabbeinu Bahya says the red came from grains with a worm inside, not from the worm's body.

sources.quote: צמר הצבוע בצבע אדום קרוי תולעת והצבע קרוי שני
sources.says: Rashbam says wool dyed red is called תולעת, and the dye is called שני.

sources.quote: ובעבור תולעת אמרו רבים כי הוא משי
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says that because of the word 'worm', many said it was silk.

sources.quote: וצבע תולעת השני אינו מגוף התולעת אלא מתוך גרגרים שהתולעת בתוכם
sources.says: Rabbeinu Bahya says the scarlet dye does not come from the worm's body but from grains the worm lives in.

25:5.headline: The תחש: a many-colored animal that lived only for a time
25:5.body: No one is sure what the תחש was. Rashi says it was an animal that existed only then, with many colors, and reads Onkelos's ססגונא as 'proud of its colors'. Rabbeinu Bahya cites the sages that it had one horn on its forehead.

sources.quote: מין חיה, ולא היתה אלא לשעה, והרבה גונים היו לה
sources.says: Rashi says it was a kind of animal that existed only for that time and had many colors.

sources.quote: לכך מתרגם ססגונא ששש ומתפאר בגונין שלו
sources.says: Rashi says Onkelos calls it ססגונא because it rejoices and takes pride in its colors.

sources.quote: וקרן אחת היה לו במצחו ולפי שעה נזדמן למשה
sources.says: Rabbeinu Bahya says it had one horn on its forehead and appeared for Moses only for a time.

25:5.headline: Acacia wood in the desert: planted by Jacob, or growing nearby?
25:5.body: Rashi asks where they found this wood in the desert. He cites a midrash that Jacob foresaw the Tabernacle and planted the trees in Egypt for his children to carry out. Bekhor Shor says there were acacia forests in the desert, which is why one place there was called Shittim.

sources.quote: ומאין היו להם במדבר? פרש רבי תנחומא: יעקב אבינו צפה ברוח הקדש
sources.says: Rashi asks where they got it in the desert, and cites Rabbi Tanchuma that Jacob foresaw it by holy spirit.

sources.quote: במדבר היו יערים שגדל שם אותו עצים הקרוין שטים
sources.says: Bekhor Shor says there were forests in the desert where the trees called שטים grew.

25:7.headline: 'Filling stones': stones that fill a setting, or whole stones?
25:7.body: Rashi says they are called stones of filling because each fills a gold socket made for it. Ramban, cited by Rabbeinu Bahya, says it means whole stones, not cut from a bigger rock, as Onkelos translates אשלמותא, wholeness.

sources.quote: ונותנין האבן שם למלאות הגמא, קרויים אבני מלואים
sources.says: Rashi says the stone is set to fill a hollow, so they are called stones of filling.

sources.quote: ופירש הרמב"ן ז"ל כי טעם מלואים שהיו שלמות, וכן תרגם אונקלוס אשלמותא
sources.says: Rabbeinu Bahya cites Ramban that מלואים means whole, as Onkelos translates it.

25:8.headline: מקדש: a holy house, or a place set for meeting?
25:8.body: Rashi reads מקדש as a house of holiness for God's name. Rashbam and Chizkuni hear in it 'a set meeting', as in התקדשו למחר, 'prepare yourselves for tomorrow': the place where God meets Israel to speak.

sources.quote: ועשו לשמי בית קדשה
sources.says: Rashi says it means make a house of holiness for my name.

sources.quote: ל' מועד שמתקדש ומזדמן אליהם לדבר
sources.says: Rashbam says it means a meeting place, where God prepares himself and comes to speak with them.

sources.quote: לשון בית מועד כמו התקדשו למחר
sources.says: Chizkuni says it means a house of meeting, as in 'prepare yourselves for tomorrow'.

25:8.headline: The years of both Temples hidden in the word 'I will dwell'
25:8.body: Rabbeinu Bahya finds both Temples in the letters of ושכנתי. It holds שכן ת"י, 'it stood 410', the years of the First Temple, and ושני ת"כ, 'and the second, 420', the years of the Second.

sources.quote: ויש במלת ושכנתי רמז למנין השנים שעמד בית ראשון ובית שני
sources.says: Rabbeinu Bahya says the word ושכנתי hints at how many years the First and Second Temples stood.

sources.quote: וזהו ושכנתי ושכן ת"י, ובית שני עמד ת"כ שנים וזה ושכנתי ושני ת"כ
sources.says: Rabbeinu Bahya says the letters spell 'dwelt 410' for the First Temple and 'the second, 420' for the Second.

25:10.headline: Only the Ark says 'they shall make', so everyone shares in Torah
25:10.body: For every other vessel God tells Moses ועשית, 'you shall make'. For the Ark it says ועשו, 'they shall make'. The midrash in Rabbeinu Bahya and Ramban says all Israel should have a part in the Ark, so all would share in the Torah inside it.

sources.quote: א"ר יהודה בר שלום אמר הקב"ה יבואו הכל ויעסקו בארון כדי שיזכו הכל בתורה
sources.says: Rabbeinu Bahya cites Rabbi Yehuda bar Shalom: God said let all come and work on the Ark, so all will merit the Torah.

sources.quote: ויתכן שירמז שיהיו כל ישראל משתתפין בעשית הארון
sources.says: Ramban says it may hint that all Israel should take part in making the Ark.

25:11.headline: The Ark's crown (זר) can also read 'stranger' (זר)
25:11.body: זר is a crown-like gold rim. Rashi says the rim on the Ark stands for the crown of Torah. A midrash in Rabbeinu Bahya notes it is spelled without a yod, so it also reads זָר, a stranger. For one who earns it the Torah is a crown, and for one who does not, it becomes a stranger.

sources.quote: והוא סימן לכתר תורה
sources.says: Rashi says the rim is a sign of the crown of Torah.

sources.quote: ונכתב זר בלא יו"ד ללמדך זכה אדם בתורה נעשית לו זר, לא זכה בתורה נעשית לו זר
sources.says: Rabbeinu Bahya says זר is written without a yod: if a person merits, the Torah is his crown; if not, it becomes a stranger to him.

25:12.headline: Did the Ark have corners, or feet?
25:12.body: Rashi follows Onkelos and reads פעמתיו as the Ark's corners. Ibn Ezra says he searched the whole Bible and never found פעם meaning a corner, only a foot. So he concludes the Ark stood on legs.

sources.quote: פעמותיו. כתרגומו זויתיה
sources.says: Rashi says it means its corners, as Onkelos translates.

sources.quote: חפשתי בכל המקרא ולא מצאתי פעם שהוא זויות, רק מלשון רגל
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says he searched all of Scripture and found פעם only meaning a foot, never a corner.

sources.quote: על כן הוצרכתי לפרש כי רגלים היו לארון
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says he therefore explains that the Ark had legs.

25:18.headline: Cherubs: children's faces, or great winged birds?
25:18.body: Rashi says the cherubs had the faces of young children. Ibn Ezra explains that the sages heard כרוב as כ־רביא, 'like a child' in Aramaic. Rashbam reads the plain sense as large winged birds, as in Ezekiel.

sources.quote: כרבים. דמות פרצוף תינוק להם
sources.says: Rashi says the cherubs had the form of a child's face.

sources.quote: ופירשו כרוביא בלשון ארמי והכ"ף משרת
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the sages explained it as Aramaic 'like a child', with the כ as a prefix.

sources.quote: כרבים - עופות, כדכתיב: (יחזקאל כח) את כרוב ממשח הסוכך. עוף גדול בעל כנפים
sources.says: Rashbam says cherubs are birds, a large winged bird, as in Ezekiel 28.

25:29.headline: מנקיות: props holding the bread, or tools for cleaning?
25:29.body: מנקיות is a rare word for one of the table's tools. Rashi follows Onkelos, 'its bearers', and says they were gold posts that held up the stacked loaves. Chizkuni reads it from נקי, clean: tools for cleaning the oven and the table.

sources.quote: ומנקיתיו. תרגומו ומכילתיה, הן סניפים כמין יתדות זהב
sources.says: Rashi says Onkelos translates it 'its holders': supports like gold pegs.

sources.quote: ומנקיתיו שהיו מנקין בהן את התנור מן הדשן ומנקין בהן את השלחן
sources.says: Chizkuni says they were used to clean the ashes from the oven and to clean the table.

25:30.headline: Why 'bread of faces'? Its shape, its quality, or its place
25:30.body: לחם פנים is literally 'bread of faces'. Rashi says the loaves had sides, 'faces', turned both ways. Rashbam says it means bread fit to set before princes. Chizkuni adds that it is so called because it is always before God.

sources.quote: לחם פנים. שהיו לו פנים כמו שפרשתי
sources.says: Rashi says it is called this because it had faces, sides, as he explained.

sources.quote: לפי פשוטו: לחם הראוי לפני שרים, לחם נאה
sources.says: Rashbam says by the plain sense it is bread fit for princes, fine bread.

sources.quote: ד״‎א כך שמו, לפי שהוא לפני תמיד
sources.says: Chizkuni gives another reason: it is named so because it is before God always.

25:34.headline: One of five verses whose grammar cannot be settled
25:34.body: It is unclear whether משקדים, 'decorated', describes the cups before it or the knobs and flowers after it. Rashi says this is one of five verses in the Torah where the reading cannot be decided.

sources.quote: זה אחד מחמשה מקראות שאין להם הכרע
sources.says: Rashi says this is one of five verses that cannot be decided.

sources.quote: אין ידוע אם גביעים משקדים או משקדים כפתוריה ופרחיה
sources.says: Rashi says it is not known whether the cups are decorated or the knobs and flowers are.

25:40.headline: 'You are being shown': God showed Moses a lampstand of fire
25:40.body: The vowels make מראה mean 'you are being shown', not 'you show', Rashi notes. He says Moses struggled with the lampstand until God showed him one made of fire. Ibn Ezra calls the word's form unusual.

sources.quote: מגיד שנתקשה משה במעשה המנורה עד שהראה לו הקב"ה מנורה של אש
sources.says: Rashi says Moses had trouble with making the lampstand until God showed him a lampstand of fire.

sources.quote: עכשו שנקוד חטף קמץ, פתרונו דאת מתחזי
sources.says: Rashi says the vowel shows it means 'that you are being shown'.

sources.quote: מלת מראה זרה ואיננה כדרך
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the form of the word מראה is strange and irregular.

26:1.headline: The curtains themselves are called the dwelling place
26:1.body: Rashbam says the ten bottom curtains are called משכן, a dwelling, because the ark, where God's presence rested, sat under them. Kli Yakar notes the verse never says 'make a dwelling', since only God can make His presence dwell.

sources.quote: עשר יריעות תחתונות קרוי משכן, כי תחתיהם הארון מקום שהשכינה שורה
sources.says: Rashbam says the ten lower curtains are called Mishkan because the ark, where the Divine Presence rests, is under them.

sources.quote: לְפִי שֶׁמִּשְׁכָּן הוּא עַל שֵׁם ״וְשָׁכַנְתִּי בְּתוֹכָם״, עַל כֵּן אֵין נָכוֹן לוֹמַר לְשׁוֹן עֲשִׂיָּה עַל שְׁכִינָתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ
sources.says: Kli Yakar says Mishkan is named for 'I will dwell among them', so it is not right to speak of making God's dwelling.

26:1.headline: Woven pictures called 'the work of a thinker'
26:1.body: חשב comes from the root for thinking and planning. Ibn Ezra says the design was first worked out in the mind and drawn on a board, and Chizkuni says weaving a picture takes thought while needlework does not.

sources.quote: כי הצורה שעלתה בלב היא חשבון, ומחשבתה, ויציירנה בלוח
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the form that rises in the heart is a calculation and a thought, which the craftsman then draws on a board.

sources.quote: זהו מעשה אריגה שצריך מחשבה אבל מעשה רוקם הוא מעשה מחט ואין צריך מחשבה
sources.says: Chizkuni says this is weaving that needs thought, while embroidery is needlework that does not.

26:6.headline: Many curtains, hooked together, become one dwelling
26:6.body: Ibn Ezra says the Tabernacle is called 'one' though made of parts, just as every body is joined from many parts and God's name is One yet includes all. Sforno says the parts stand at different ranks but are set in one order to do God's will.

sources.quote: והמשכן קראו אחד כולל הכל, כי כל גוף אינו דבר אחד, רק הוא מחובר מאחדים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the Tabernacle is called one as a whole, since no body is a single thing but is joined from many units.

sources.quote: וככה השם הנכבד שהוא אחד כולל הכל ונקרא אחד
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the same is true of God's honored name, which is one, includes all, and is called One.

sources.quote: כִּי עִם הֱיוֹת הַמַּדְרֵגוֹת בִּלְתִּי שָׁווֹת, הֵן אָמְנָם מְסֻדָּרוֹת בְּסֵדֶר אֶחָד לַעֲשׂוֹת רְצוֹן קוֹנָם
sources.says: Sforno says that though the levels are unequal, they are arranged in one order to do their Maker's will.

26:9.headline: The folded curtain covers the doorway like a bride's veil
26:9.body: The extra curtain is doubled over the front, the 'face' of the tent. Rashi says it looked like a modest bride covering her face with a veil.

sources.quote: חֲצִי רָחְבָּה הָיָה תָלוּי וְכָפוּל עַל הַמָּסָךְ שֶׁבַּמִּזְרָח כְּנֶגֶד הַפֶּתַח, דּוֹמֶה לְכַלָּה צְנוּעָה הַמְכֻסָּה בְּצָעִיף עַל פָּנֶיהָ
sources.says: Rashi says half its width hung doubled over the eastern screen by the door, like a modest bride who covers her face with a veil.

26:12.headline: The overhanging cloth trails behind like a noblewoman's hem
26:12.body: תסרח means the cloth hangs over and trails down the back. Chizkuni quotes the school of Rabbi Yishmael: the Tabernacle is like a great lady walking in the market with her skirts trailing behind her.

sources.quote: תנא דבי רבי ישמעאל למה משכן דומה למטרוניתא מהלכת בשוק ושיפוליה מהלכין אחריה
sources.says: Chizkuni cites the school of Rabbi Yishmael: the Tabernacle is like a noblewoman walking in the market with her hems trailing after her.

26:15.headline: 'The boards': wood Jacob planted in Egypt long before
26:15.body: The verse says 'the boards', as if they were already known. Rashi says Jacob planted cedars in Egypt and told his sons to take them along when they left, for the Tabernacle God would command.

sources.quote: הָיָה לוֹ לוֹמַר וְעָשִׂיתָ קְרָשִׁים, כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר בְּכָל דָּבָר וְדָבָר, מַהוּ הַקְּרָשִׁים? מֵאוֹתָן הָעוֹמְדִין וּמְיֻחָדִין לְכָךְ; יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ נָטַע אֲרָזִים בְּמִצְרַיִם
sources.says: Rashi asks why it says 'the boards' and not 'boards', and answers: the ones set aside for this, since Jacob planted cedars in Egypt.

sources.quote: וְאָמַר לָהֶם שֶׁעָתִיד הַקָּבָּ"ה לְצַוּוֹת אוֹתָן לַעֲשׂוֹת מִשְׁכָּן בַּמִּדְבָּר מֵעֲצֵי שִׁטִּים, רְאוּ שֶׁיִּהְיוּ מְזֻמָּנִים בְּיֶדְכֶם
sources.says: Rashi says Jacob told his sons God would command them to build a Tabernacle of acacia wood in the desert, so they should have it ready.

sources.quote: ומה שהזכירה בה"א הידיעה לרמוז על הקרשים שהוציאום ישראל ממצרים
sources.says: Bahya says the word has 'the' to point to the boards Israel brought out of Egypt.

26:15.headline: Acacia wood, named like the place where Israel sinned
26:15.body: Bahya says God chose wood called שטים because Israel sinned and was struck at a place called Shittim, so they would be healed through שטים. Kli Yakar cites a midrash that the wood atones for the שטות, the folly, of the golden calf.

sources.quote: לפי שישראל חטאו בשטים לקו בשטים ונתרפאו בשטים
sources.says: Bahya says Israel sinned at Shittim, was struck at Shittim, and was healed through shittim wood.

sources.quote: עֲצֵי שִׁטִּים לְכַפֵּר עַל שְׁטוּת מַעֲשֵׂה הָעֵגֶל
sources.says: Kli Yakar cites a midrash that shittim wood atones for the folly of the golden calf.

26:18.headline: The south is named for being dried out by heat
26:18.body: Ramban says נגב, south, comes from being dry from the heat. The verse then adds תימנה, the plain name for south, to explain the nickname.

sources.quote: וְיִקְרָא הַדָּרוֹם "נֶגֶב", בִּהְיוֹתוֹ נָגוּב מִפְּנֵי הַחֹם
sources.says: Ramban says the south is called negev because it is dried out by the heat.

sources.quote: וְאָמַר "נֶגְבָּה", בְּכִנּוּי, וִיבָאֵר "תֵּימָנָה", הוּא הַשֵּׁם
sources.says: Ramban says the verse uses נגבה as a nickname and explains it with תימנה, the proper name.

26:20.headline: North is 'the hidden side', where the sun never shows
26:20.body: Ramban says צפון, north, comes from the word for hidden, because the sun is never seen in that direction.

sources.quote: וְהַצָּפוֹן יַזְכִּירֶנּוּ (שמות כ"ו:כ') בִּשְׁמוֹ. וְנִקְרָא כֵן כִּי הוּא צָפוּן, אֵין הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ נִרְאֶה בּוֹ לְעוֹלָם
sources.says: Ramban says the north, named in this verse, is called tzafon because it is hidden: the sun is never seen in it.

26:24.headline: Spelled like 'perfect', but here it means 'twins'
26:24.body: תמים usually means whole or perfect. Rashi says here it means the same as תואמים, twins, the word used earlier in the verse for boards fitted side by side.

sources.quote: ויחדו יהיו תמים. כְּמוֹ תוֹאֲמִים
sources.says: Rashi says תמים here is like תואמים, twins.

sources.quote: כָּל הַקְּרָשִׁים תּוֹאֲמִים זֶה לָזֶה מִלְּמַטָּה
sources.says: Rashi says all the boards are matched to one another at the bottom.

26:31.headline: The curtain is a screen between a king and his people
26:31.body: Rashi says פרכת means a partition. In the sages' language it is a פרגוד, the screen that separates a king from the public.

sources.quote: לְשׁוֹן מְחִצָּה הוּא, וּבִלְשׁוֹן חֲכָמִים פַּרְגּוֹד דָּבָר הַמַּבְדִּיל בֵּין הַמֶּלֶךְ וּבֵין הָעָם
sources.says: Rashi says it means a partition, and in the sages' language a pargod, a thing that separates the king from the people.

sources.quote: לפי ענינו לשון מחיצה והבדלה בין בית לבית
sources.says: Rashbam says, from its context, it means a partition between one room and another.

27:1.headline: The four letters of 'altar' spell what it brings
27:1.body: A midrash reads each letter of מזבח, altar, as the first letter of a word: forgiveness, merit, blessing, and life.

sources.quote: מהו מזבח? מ' מחילה, ז' זכות, ב' ברכה, ח' חיים
sources.says: The Tanchuma reads the letters of מזבח as forgiveness, merit, blessing and life.

27:2.headline: Copper on the altar answers a forehead of copper
27:2.body: Rashi says the altar is covered in נחשת, copper, to atone for a brazen face. Isaiah calls a stubborn people's forehead copper.

sources.quote: לכפר על עזות מצח, שנ' ומצחך נחושה
sources.says: Rashi says the copper atones for a brazen forehead, as Isaiah says 'your forehead is copper'.

sources.quote: מזבח הנחשת מכפר על מצח נחושה
sources.says: Bahya quotes a midrash: the copper altar atones for a forehead of copper.

27:8.headline: Hollow, like an empty-headed man
27:8.body: The altar is hollow inside, נבוב. Commentators link it to Job's phrase about a hollow man who gains a heart, an empty person who later gains sense.

sources.quote: ואיש נבוב ילבב
sources.says: Ibn Ezra compares the word to Job's 'a hollow man will gain a heart'.

sources.quote: שהוא ריק בלי לבב על דרך האומרים ראש בלי מוח
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says that man is empty, without a heart, like people say 'a head without a brain'.

sources.quote: כי האדם בילדותו הוא חלול מבלי דעת והשכל
sources.says: Bahya says a person in youth is hollow, without knowledge, and later gains a heart.

27:10.headline: Silver bands, from a word that also means longing
27:10.body: Rashi says חשוק means a belt that wraps the pillar. Ibn Ezra says it means what clings, the same root as a soul that longs and clings to someone.

sources.quote: אך יודע אני שחשוק לשון חגורה
sources.says: Rashi says he knows חשוק means a belt.

sources.quote: כי ותדבק נפשו (ברא' לד ג) כמו חשקה נפשו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the bands cling to the pillars, as 'his soul clung' is like 'his soul longed'.

27:13.headline: East is called 'the front'
27:13.body: Rashi says קדם means front, so the east is the front and the west is the back. That is why the Mediterranean is called 'the back sea'.

sources.quote: קדם לשון פנים, אחור לשון אחורים, לפיכך המזרח קרוי קדם
sources.says: Rashi says קדם means front and אחור means back, so the east is called קדם.

27:19.headline: Rashi lets the name settle how the pegs worked
27:19.body: Rashi was not sure if the pegs were driven into the ground or just hung as weights. He decides from the name יתד, a stake, that they were driven in.

sources.quote: ואומר אני ששמן מוכיח עליהם שהם תקועים בארץ, לכך נקראו יתדות
sources.says: Rashi says their name shows they were stuck in the ground, which is why they are called יתדות.

27:20.headline: Israel is like an olive: it gives its oil when pressed
27:20.body: The midrash asks why Israel is compared to the olive. An olive is beaten and crushed before it gives oil, and Israel too is beaten and then turns back to God.

sources.quote: אלא מה הזית הזה, עד שהוא באילנו מגרגרין אותו ואחר כך מורידין אותו מן הזית ונחבט
sources.says: The midrash says the olive is picked, brought down and beaten before it gives oil.

sources.quote: ואחר כך עושין תשובה והקדוש ברוך הוא עונה להם
sources.says: It says Israel, beaten by the nations, then repents and God answers them.

27:20.headline: Crushed oil, a hint of the two Temples
27:20.body: A midrash in Bahya ties כתית, crushed, to the first and second Temples, which stood 410 and 420 years. Bahya adds that crushing hints that both would be destroyed.

sources.quote: ובמדרש כתית זה מקדש ראשון שעמד ת"י שנה מקדש שני ת"כ שנה
sources.says: Bahya quotes a midrash that כתית is the first Temple, which stood 410 years, and the second, which stood 420.

sources.quote: לכך נאמר הרמז בשניהם בלשון כתית שהוא לשון כתישה ומרמס
sources.says: Bahya says the hint uses כתית, a word of crushing and trampling, since both were to be destroyed.

28:4.headline: Rashi admits he never learned what the ephod looked like
28:4.body: Rashi says no teacher or old text told him the shape of the ephod, so he works it out from other verses. He decides it was a kind of apron tied behind, named from the verb ויאפד, to adorn.

sources.quote: לֹא שָׁמַעְתִּי וְלֹא מָצָאתִי בַּבָּרַיְתָא פֵּרוּשׁ תַּבְנִיתוֹ, וְלִבִּי אוֹמֵר לִי שֶׁהוּא חֲגוֹרָה לוֹ מֵאֲחוֹרָיו
sources.says: Rashi says he never heard or found its shape described, and his heart tells him it was a belt-like garment tied behind.

sources.quote: עַל שֵׁם שֶׁאוֹפְדוֹ וּמְקַשְּׁטוֹ בוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says it is called ephod because the priest is girded and adorned with it.

28:4.headline: A word used once, read from the gold settings for gems
28:4.body: תשבץ appears only here. Rashi reads it from משבצות, the little gold sockets that hold gems, so the tunic was woven with a pattern of small hollows.

sources.quote: עֲשׂוּיִין מִשְׁבְּצוֹת לְנוֹי, וְהַמִּשְׁבְּצוֹת הֵם כְּמִין גֻּמּוֹת הָעֲשׂוּיוֹת בְּתַכְשִׁיטֵי זָהָב לְמוֹשַׁב קְבִיעַת אֲבָנִים טוֹבוֹת
sources.says: Rashi says it was made with decorative settings, like the hollows in gold jewelry that hold precious stones.

sources.quote: כעין גומות גומות הוא עשוי
sources.says: Rashbam says it was made like rows of little hollows.

28:15.headline: Why the breastplate is called the breastplate of judgment
28:15.body: משפט can mean a court ruling or a clear decision. Rashi says the breastplate atones for bad rulings, or that it gives clear answers. Rashbam says it is named for the Urim inside it, which told Israel what to do.

sources.quote: שֶׁמְּכַפֵּר עַל קִלְקוּל הַדִּין. דָּ"אַ, מִשְׁפָּט שֶׁמְּבָרֵר דְּבָרָיו וְהַבְטָחָתוֹ אֱמֶת
sources.says: Rashi says it atones for corrupted judgment, or else it is called משפט because it makes its words clear and its promise true.

sources.quote: לפי שנותנים בהם האורים והתומים שמגידים משפט ישראל וצרכיהם
sources.says: Rashbam says it is named for the Urim and Tumim placed in it, which tell Israel its judgment and needs.

28:17.headline: Reuben's red stone, spelled like the word for a man
28:17.body: Rabbeinu Bahya says the red stone אדם went to Reuben because his face reddened with shame over Bilhah. He adds that it is spelled without a ו so it also reads אדם, a man, hinting at the human-shaped mandrakes Reuben found.

sources.quote: ומה שנתן אבן אודם לראובן על שם שהאדימו פניו בחטא בלהה
sources.says: Bahya says the red stone was given to Reuben because his face reddened over his sin with Bilhah.

sources.quote: כדודאים שמצא ראובן ששם דמות אדם ועל כן נכתב אדם חסר וי"ו להורות על אדם
sources.says: Bahya says the word is written without a ו to point to אדם, a man, like the mandrakes Reuben found that have a human shape.

28:18.headline: The stone יהלם may be named for striking and breaking
28:18.body: Ibn Ezra cites a Spanish sage who says יהלם is the stone that breaks all other stones. He reads the name from הולם, to strike, with an extra י at the start.

sources.quote: יהלום הוא הנקרא אלמם שהוא שובר כל האבנים, ונוקב הבדולח מגזרת הולם פעם
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says יהלום is the stone that breaks all stones and pierces crystal, from the root of הולם, to strike.

28:19.headline: A stone of dreams, or a stone of strength
28:19.body: Ibn Ezra reads אחלמה from חלום, a dream: whoever wears it sees dreams. Rabbeinu Bahya reads it from a word for strength: it steadies the heart of someone going to war.

sources.quote: גם אחלמה, אל חלמה, והוא אבן שכל מי שהאבן ההיא באצבעו לעולם יראה חלומות
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says אחלמה is a stone that makes whoever wears it on his finger always see dreams.

sources.quote: וסגולת האבן הזאת שמחזקת את הלב שלא ירך בלכתו למלחמה ולכך נקראת אחלמה מלשון חוזק
sources.says: Bahya says it strengthens the heart in war, so it is called אחלמה, from a word for strength.

28:22.headline: Chains that hold like the roots of a tree
28:22.body: Rashi reads שרשת from שרשים, roots. Roots hold a tree in the ground, and these chains hold the breastplate to the ephod. He rejects Menachem's view that the longer word שרשרת also means roots: that one just means a chain.

sources.quote: לְשׁוֹן שָׁרְשֵׁי אִילָן, הַמְאַחֲזִין לָאִילָן לְהֵאָחֵז וּלְהִתָּקַע בָּאָרֶץ, אַף אֵלּוּ יִהְיוּ מְאַחֲזִין לַחֹשֶׁן
sources.says: Rashi says it is from the roots of a tree that hold it in the earth, and these too hold the breastplate.

sources.quote: וְאֵינִי רוֹאֶה אֶת דְּבָרָיו, אֶלָּא שַׁרְשֶׁרֶת בִּלְשׁוֹן עִבְרִית כְּשַׁלְשֶׁלֶת בִּלְשׁוֹן מִשְׁנָה
sources.says: Rashi says he does not accept Menachem's reading, and that שרשרת in Hebrew is a chain, like שלשלת in the Mishnah.

28:30.headline: Urim lights up the letters, Tumim makes the answer whole
28:30.body: Rashi says the Urim and Tumim made the breastplate's words light up and come out complete. Ramban explains: letters on the stones lit up before the priest, and the Tumim let him put them in the right order to read the answer.

sources.quote: שֶׁעַל יָדוֹ הוּא מֵאִיר דְּבָרָיו וּמְתַמֵּם אֶת דְּבָרָיו
sources.says: Rashi says that through it the breastplate lights up its words and makes them complete.

sources.quote: כִּי הָיוּ שֵׁמוֹת קְדוֹשִׁים, מִכֹּחָם יָאִירוּ הָאוֹתִיּוֹת מֵאַבְנֵי הַחֹשֶׁן אֶל עֵינֵי הַכֹּהֵן הַשּׁוֹאֵל בְּמִשְׁפָּטָם
sources.says: Ramban says they were holy names that made letters on the breastplate stones light up before the priest who asked.

sources.quote: אֲבָל הָיוּ שָׁם שְׁמוֹת הַקֹּדֶשׁ אֲחֵרִים נִקְרָאִים "תֻּמִּים", מִכֹּחָם יִהְיֶה לֵב הַכֹּהֵן תָּמִים בִּידִיעַת עִנְיַן הָאוֹתִיּוֹת שֶׁהֵאִירוּ לְעֵינָיו
sources.says: Ramban says other holy names, the Tumim, made the priest's heart whole in knowing what the lit letters meant.

28:32.headline: Not to be torn, or not to be cut open
28:32.body: Rashi reads לא יקרע as a law: whoever tears the robe breaks a commandment. Sforno reads יקרע as cutting an opening, as in cutting windows, so the neck hole must be round and not slit down the front.

sources.quote: כְּדֵי שֶׁלֹּא יִקָּרֵעַ; וְהַקּוֹרְעוֹ עוֹבֵר בְּלָאו
sources.says: Rashi says it is so the robe will not tear, and whoever tears it breaks a prohibition.

sources.quote: לֹא יִהְיֶה לוֹ בֵּית הַצַּוָּאר נִפְתָּח לְאָרְכּוֹ לְפָנָיו, אֲבָל יִהְיֶה עָגוֹל
sources.says: Sforno says the neck opening should not be slit lengthwise in front but should be round.

sources.quote: וּלְשׁוֹן יִקָּרֵעַ יֵאָמֵר עַל הַדָּבָר הַפָּתוּחַ לְאָרְכּוֹ, כְּמוֹ "וְקָרַע לוֹ חַלּוֹנָי
sources.says: Sforno says יקרע is used for a long opening, as in cutting windows.

28:36.headline: The gold plate is named for the place people look
28:36.body: Rashbam says the gold plate is called ציץ because it sits on the forehead, where people look, as in מציץ, peering. Chizkuni says it is named for shining, as in נוצצים, sparkling.

sources.quote: לפי שנותנו על מצח מקום ראיית בני אדם קרוי ציץ, כמו: מציץ מן החרכים
sources.says: Rashbam says it is called ציץ because it is put on the forehead, where people look, as in peering through the lattice.

sources.quote: אולי הכל מגזרת ציץ דבר נראה, וככה מציץ מן החרכים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra suggests ציץ means something seen, as in peering through the lattice.

sources.quote: מין תכשיט מאיר ומזהיר כמו ונוצצים
sources.says: Chizkuni says it is a shining ornament, as in the word for sparkling.

28:38.headline: Aaron forgives sin by carrying it
28:38.body: נשא can mean to forgive or to carry. Rashi says here it means forgiveness, yet it keeps its plain sense too: Aaron carries the load of the sin and so lifts it off the offerings.

sources.quote: לְשׁוֹן סְלִיחָה; וְאַעַפִּ"כֵ אֵינוֹ זָז מִמַּשְׁמָעוֹ – אַהֲרֹן נוֹשֵׂא אֶת הַמַּשָּׂא שֶׁל עָוֹן
sources.says: Rashi says it means forgiveness, but it does not leave its plain meaning: Aaron carries the burden of the sin.

28:41.headline: Fill their hands: install them, or make them whole
28:41.body: Rashi says filling the hands means installing someone in office, like a ruler handing over a leather glove. Ramban rejects this and says it means making the hand complete, fit for every service. Onkelos translates it as bringing their offerings.

sources.quote: כָּל מִלּוּי יָדַיִם לְשׁוֹן חִנּוּךְ
sources.says: Rashi says every use of filling the hands means installing someone.

sources.quote: נוֹתֵן הַשַּׁלִּיט בְּיָדוֹ בֵּית יָד שֶׁל עוֹר
sources.says: Rashi says that in his language, the ruler puts a leather glove in the hand of the person being appointed.

sources.quote: וְהַנָּכוֹן בִּלְשׁוֹן מִלּוּי יָדַיִם בַּתּוֹרָה שֶׁהוּא לְשׁוֹן שְׁלֵמוּת
sources.says: Ramban says the right reading is that filling the hands means completeness.

sources.quote: וּתְקָרֵב יָת קֻרְבַּנְהוֹן
sources.says: Onkelos translates it as: and you shall offer their offering.

29:1.headline: Why a bull? Rashi says it atones for the golden calf
29:1.body: The priests' installation starts with a bull. Rashi says a bull was chosen to make up for the golden calf, which was itself a young bull. Ramban agrees that this offering atoned for the calf.

sources.quote: לכפר על מעשה העגל שהוא פר
sources.says: Rashi says the bull atones for the sin of the calf, which was a bull.

sources.quote: והיה פר חטאת זה לכפר על מעשה העגל
sources.says: Ramban says this sin-offering bull came to atone for the sin of the calf.

29:18.headline: A 'pleasing smell' means God is pleased his word was done
29:18.body: ריח ניחוח sounds like a pleasant smell. Rashi reads ניחוח as נחת רוח, contentment: God is pleased because what he said was carried out. Ibn Ezra notes the doubled ח and hints at a secret about the soul.

sources.quote: נחת רוח לפני, שאמרתי ונעשה רצוני
sources.says: Rashi says it means contentment before God, because he spoke and his will was done.

sources.quote: כפל החי"ת והמבין סוד נשמת האדם יבין זה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra notes the ח is doubled and says one who knows the secret of the human soul will understand.

29:24.headline: Waving the offering toward the God of every direction
29:24.body: תנופה is moving the offering to and fro and up and down. Rashi stops to explain the motion: side to side for the One who owns the four winds, up and down for the One who owns heaven and earth. Onkelos simply calls it a lifting.

sources.quote: מוליך ומביא למי שארבע רוחות העולם שלו
sources.says: Rashi says the priest moves it to and fro for the One to whom the four directions belong.

sources.quote: מעלה ומוריד למי שהשמים והארץ שלו
sources.says: Rashi says he raises and lowers it for the One to whom heaven and earth belong.

sources.quote: ותרים יתהון ארמותא
sources.says: Onkelos translates the waving as 'you shall lift them as a lifting'.

29:27.headline: Waving and lifting: two acts, or one said two ways?
29:27.body: The verse speaks of the breast that was waved and the thigh that was lifted, תרומה. Rashi and Ibn Ezra treat them as two different motions. Bekhor Shor says they are one act, named twice only to vary the Hebrew.

sources.quote: הורם. לשון מעלה ומוריד
sources.says: Rashi says הורם means raising and lowering.

sources.quote: ואין הונף כמו הורם, כי יורם למעלה ולא יונף
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says waving is not the same as lifting, since a thing can be lifted up without being waved.

sources.quote: תנופה ותרומה. אחד הוא אלא לצחצח לשון עברי
sources.says: Bekhor Shor says waving and lifting are one thing, and the two words only polish the Hebrew style.

29:36.headline: Here חטא means to purify, not to sin
29:36.body: The root חטא usually means sin. Here it means the opposite: to cleanse the altar. Rashi and Onkelos render it 'you shall purify', done by putting blood on it with a finger.

sources.quote: ותדכי, לשון מתנת דמים הנתונים באצבע קרוי חטוי
sources.says: Rashi says it means 'you shall purify', and putting blood on with a finger is called חטוי.

sources.quote: ותדכי על מדבחא
sources.says: Onkelos translates it 'you shall purify the altar'.

sources.quote: והמפרשים אמרו כי וחטאת כמו וטהרת
sources.says: Ibn Ezra reports that commentators say וחטאת means 'you shall purify'.

29:37.headline: Whatever touches the altar becomes holy, or must be holy first?
29:37.body: יקדש can mean 'becomes holy' or 'must make itself holy'. Rashi says the altar makes holy what is placed on it, so even a flawed offering is not taken down. Rashbam and Chizkuni say whoever comes near must first make himself holy.

sources.quote: אפלו קרבן פסול שעלה עליו קדשו המזבח להכשירו שלא ירד
sources.says: Rashi says even an unfit offering that went up on the altar is made holy by it, so it is not taken down.

sources.quote: וקרב אל המזבח יקדש תחילה בטרם יקרב אל המזבח
sources.says: Rashbam says one who comes near the altar must first make himself holy.

sources.quote: כל הרוצה ליגע בו יזמן ויטהר עצמו מקודם לכן
sources.says: Chizkuni says anyone who wants to touch it must prepare and purify himself first.

3:2.headline: The flame has a heart
3:2.body: Rashi reads בלבת as “in the heart of the fire.” Maimonides uses this verse to explain how לב, “heart,” can mean the middle of something.

sources.quote: בלבת אש. בְּשַׁלְהֶבֶת אֵשׁ – לִבּוֹ שֶׁל אֵשׁ, כְּמוֹ "לֵב הַשָּׁמַיִם" (דברים ד'), "בְּלֵב הָאֵלָה" (שמואל ב י"ח);
sources.says: Rashi explains בלבת אש as the heart of the fire and compares other uses of לב.

sources.quote: וכיוון שהאבר הזה נמצא באמצע הגוף, הושאל לאמצעו של כל דבר: "עַד לֵב הַשָּׁמַיִם" (דברים ד,יא), "לַבַּת אֵשׁ" (שמות ג,ב).
sources.says: Maimonides says the word for heart extends to the middle of anything and cites this verse.

3:2.headline: The thornbush shows God sharing Israel’s pain
3:2.body: Rashi asks why the revelation comes from הסנה, a thornbush, rather than another tree. Shemot Rabbah says speaking from among thorns shows God sharing Israel’s suffering.

sources.quote: מתוך הסנה. וְלֹא אִילָן אַחֵר, מִשּׁוּם "עִמּוֹ אָנֹכִי בְצָרָה" (תהילים צא טו):
sources.says: Rashi explains the choice of the thornbush through God being with the sufferer.

sources.quote: אָמַר לוֹ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לְמשֶׁה, אִי אַתָּה מַרְגִּישׁ שֶׁאֲנִי שָׁרוּי בְּצַעַר כְּשֵׁם שֶׁיִּשְׂרָאֵל שְׁרוּיִם בְּצַעַר, הֱוֵי יוֹדֵעַ מִמָּקוֹם שֶׁאֲנִי מְדַבֵּר עִמְּךָ מִתּוֹךְ הַקּוֹצִים כִּבְיָכוֹל אֲנִי שֻׁתָּף בְּצַעֲרָן.
sources.says: Shemot Rabbah says God speaks from among thorns to show that he shares Israel’s pain.

3:3.headline: Turning aside brings Moses closer
3:3.body: Ibn Ezra explains that סור can mean moving away or turning toward someone, depending on the words around it. Here אסרה means Moses will leave his position and approach the bush.

sources.quote: ויאמר משה אסרה נא. גזרת סר אם בא אחריה מ"ם היה למרחוק כמו סורו ממני (תה' ו ט), הוא אומר להם רחקו ממני, ואם אחריה "אֶל" בשלש נקודות תהפך הדבר כמו סורו אלי (שופ' ד יח) סור ממקומך ובא אלי, שיסור ממקומו ויקרב אל מקום הסנה:
sources.says: Ibn Ezra contrasts turning away with turning toward and says Moses approaches the bush.

3:6.headline: Looking can mean trying to understand
3:6.body: Maimonides explains that הביט can mean looking with the eyes or directing the mind toward something. He reads מהביט אל האלהים here as trying to understand God.

sources.quote: ב) והושאל לפניית הדעת והכוונתה לעיין בדבר כדי שתשיג אותו, והוא שנאמר: "לֹא הִבִּיט אָוֶן בְּיַעֲקֹב" (במדבר כג,כא), כי האָוֶן אינו נראה בעין. וכיוצא בזה דבריו: "וְהִבִּיטוּ אַחֲרֵי מֹשֶׁה [עַד בֹּאוֹ הָאֹהֱלָה]" (שמות לג,ח), אמרו החכמים ז"ל שיש בו גם המשמעות הזו, ושזו הודעה על כך שהם עקבו אחרי מעשיו ודבריו והתבוננו בהם. במשמעות זו נאמר: "הַבֶּט נָא הַשָּׁמַיְמָה" (בראשית טו,ה), משום שזה היה במראה הנבואה. ובהשאלה זו כל לשון הבטה שנאמר לגבי האל יתעלה: "[כִּי יָרֵא] מֵהַבִּיט אֶל הָאֱלֹהִים" (שמות ג,ו), "וּתְמֻנַת ה' יַבִּיט" (במדבר יב,ח), "וְהַבִּיט אֶל עָמָל לֹא תוּכָל" (חבקוק א,יג).
sources.says: Maimonides includes this verse among uses of הביט that mean mental attention.

3:7.headline: Knowing their pain means paying attention to it
3:7.body: Rashi reads ידעתי as God giving close attention to Israel’s suffering. The word expresses concern for their cries, beyond simply knowing the facts.

sources.quote: כי ידעתי את מכאביו. כְּמוֹ "וַיֵּדַע אֱלֹהִים" (שמות ב'), כְּלוֹמַר כִּי שַׂמְתִּי לֵב לְהִתְבּוֹנֵן וְלָדַעַת אֶת מַכְאוֹבָיו וְלֹא הֶעֱלַמְתִּי עֵינַי לֶאֱטֹם אָזְנַי מִצַּעֲקָתָם:
sources.says: Rashi says God attends to their pain and has not shut his eyes or ears to their cries.

3:14.headline: A name read as a promise or as existence itself
3:14.body: Rashi reads אהיה, “I will be,” as a promise to stay with Israel through suffering. Maimonides reads אהיה אשר אהיה as saying that God must exist and cannot cease to exist.

sources.quote: אהיה אשר אהיה. אֶהְיֶה עִמָּם בְּצָרָה זוֹ אֲשֶׁר אֶהְיֶה עִמָּם בְּשִׁעְבּוּד שְׁאָר מַלְכֻיּוֹת.
sources.says: Rashi explains the name as God being with Israel in this suffering and in future oppression.

sources.quote: נמצא שסיכום העניין הזה ופירושו הגיע לכדי כך: "המצוי אשר הוא המצוי", כלומר מחויב המציאות. זה מה שההוכחה מביאה אליו, שיש דבר מחויב המציאות שאינו נעדר ולא ייעדר,
sources.says: Maimonides says the name means that God must exist and can never cease to exist.

3:15.headline: A missing letter turns “forever” toward “conceal it”
3:15.body: Rashi notices that לעלם, “forever,” is written without ו. He connects that spelling with העלימהו, “conceal it,” to explain why God’s name is not pronounced as written.

sources.quote: זה שמי לעלם. חָסֵר וָי"ו, לוֹמַר, הַעֲלִימֵהוּ – שֶׁלֹּא יִקָּרֵא כִּכְתָבוֹ (פסחים נ'):
sources.says: Rashi reads the missing ו as a hint to conceal the written pronunciation of God’s name.

3:16.headline: These words are an old sign of coming freedom
3:16.body: Rashi says Jacob and Joseph had taught Israel to recognize the wording פקד, “take notice,” as a sign of rescue. Moses uses that wording in פקד פקדתי.

sources.quote: ושמעו לקלך. מִכֵּיוָן שֶׁתֹּאמַר לָהֶם לָשׁוֹן זֶה, יִשְׁמְעוּ לְקוֹלְךָ, שֶׁכְּבָר סִימָן זֶה מָסוּר בְּיָדָם מִיַּעֲקֹב וּמִיּוֹסֵף, שֶׁבְּלָשׁוֹן זֶה הֵם נִגְאָלִים, יַעֲקֹב אָמַר לָהֶם "וֵאלֹהִים פָּקֹד יִפְקֹד אֶתְכֶם" (בראשית נ'), יוֹסֵף אָמַר לָהֶם "פָּקֹד יִפְקֹד אֱלֹהִים אֶתְכֶם" (שם):
sources.says: Rashi says Jacob and Joseph passed down this wording as a sign of Israel’s coming rescue.

3:19.headline: Will a strong hand make Pharaoh yield?
3:19.body: Rashi reads ולא ביד חזקה as “unless I show him my strong hand.” Sforno reads it as “not even under a strong hand,” because God will harden Pharaoh’s heart when the plagues stop.

sources.quote: לא יתן אתכם מלך מצרים להלך. אִם אֵין אֲנִי מַרְאֶה לוֹ יָדִי הַחֲזָקָה; כְּלוֹמַר, כָּל עוֹד שֶׁאֵין אֲנִי מוֹדִיעוֹ יָדִי הַחֲזָקָה, לֹא יִתֵּן אֶתְכֶם לַהֲלֹךְ:
sources.says: Rashi says Pharaoh will refuse as long as God has not shown him his strong hand.

sources.quote: וְלֹא בְּיָד חֲזָקָה. וַאֲנִי אֶעֱשֶׂה שֶׁלֹּא יִתֵּן אֶתְכֶם לַהֲלוֹךְ כַּאֲשֶׁר תֶּחֱזַק יָדִי עָלָיו, כִּי בְּסוּר הַמַּכּוֹת אֲחַזֵּק לִבּוֹ שֶׁלֹּא יִירָא שֶׁאוֹסִיף לְהַכּוֹתוֹ:
sources.says: Sforno says Pharaoh will still refuse under God’s strong hand because his heart will be hardened when the plagues cease.

3:22.headline: Asking for gifts or borrowing changes what is owed
3:22.body: Rabbeinu Bahya reads ושאלה as asking for gifts, which need not be returned. Sforno reads it as borrowing, with ownership passing to Israel later when Egypt attacks them.

sources.quote: ושאלה אשה משכנתה. ח"ו שיתיר הקב"ה לגנוב דעת הבריות שישאלו מהם כלי כסף וכלי זהב ולא ישיבו להם, אבל לשון ושאלה הוא שתתן לה במתנה שכן מצינו בגדעון (שופטים ח׳:כ״ד) ויאמר אליהם גדעון אשאלה מכם שאלה ותתנו לי איש נזם שללו כי נזמי זהב להם כי ישמעאלים הם, וכן מצינו בבת שבע (מלכים א ב׳:כ׳) שאלה אחת קטנה אנכי שואלת מאתך יותן את אבישג השונמית הרי מתנה שנקראת בלשון שאלה.
sources.says: Rabbeinu Bahya says ושאלה means requesting a gift and gives other biblical examples.

sources.quote: וְנִצַּלְתֶּם אֶת מִצְרָיִם. אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁתְּקַבְּלוּ הַכֹּל מֵהֶם דֶּרֶךְ הַשְׁאֵלָה, וְתִהְיוּ חַיָּבִים לְהַחֲזִיר, הִנֵּה תִּקְנוּ אַחַר כָּךְ אֶת הַכֹּל בַּדִּין, בְּרָדְפָם אַחֲרֵיכֶם לְהִלָּחֵם בָּכֶם וְלִשְׁלֹל אֶת שְׁלַלְכֶם.
sources.says: Sforno says the goods begin as loans but later become Israel’s property when the Egyptians attack.

3:22.headline: The vowels show who empties Egypt
3:22.body: Rashi reads ונצלתם as “you will empty out” Egypt. He uses its vowels and the letter נ to show that the Israelites perform the action, rather than have it done to them.
