sources.quote: ונצלתם. כְּתַרְגוּמוֹ "וּתְרוֹקִנוּן", וְכֵן "וַיְּנַצְּלוּ אֶת מִצְרָיִם" (שמות י"ב), "וַיִּתְנַצְּלוּ בְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל אֶת עֶדְיָם" (שם ל"ג), וְהַנּוּ"ן בּוֹ יְסוֹד; וּמְנַחֵם חִבְּרוֹ בְּמַחְבֶּרֶת צָדִ"י עִם "וַיַּצֵּל אֱלֹהִים אֶת מִקְנֵה אֲבִיכֶם", "אֲשֶׁר הִצִּיל אֱלֹהִים מֵאָבִינוּ" (בראשית ל"א), וְלֹא יֵאָמְנוּ דְּבָרָיו, כִּי אִם לֹא הָיְתָה הַנּוּ"ן יְסוֹד וְהִיא נְקוּדָה בְחִירִק, לֹא תְהֵא מְשַׁמֶּשֶׁת בִּלְשׁוֹן וּפְעַלְתֶּם אֶלָּא בִּלְשׁוֹן וְנִפְעַלְתֶּם,
sources.says: Rashi explains the word as emptying out and uses its נ and vowels to show who performs the action.

30:12.headline: 'Lift the head' of Israel means take a count
30:12.body: כי תשא את ראש reads literally 'when you lift the head'. Rashi says it means 'receive', to take the total of a count. A midrash quoted by Bahya also hears 'raise up' in it: this is how Israel's horn will be raised.

sources.quote: כי תשא. לְשׁוֹן קַבָּלָה, כְּתַרְגּוּמוֹ; כְּשֶׁתַּחְפֹּץ לְקַבֵּל סְכוּם מִנְיָנָם לָדַעַת כַּמָּה הֵם
sources.says: Rashi says תשא means receiving, as the Aramaic has it: when you want to take the total of their number.

sources.quote: כי תשא את ראש. נשיאות ראש קרוי כשמונין אותם
sources.says: Bekhor Shor says counting people is called 'lifting the head'.

sources.quote: אמר לו הקב"ה למשה במה תרום קרנם של ישראל בכי תשא
sources.says: Bahya cites a midrash in which God tells Moses that Israel's horn will be raised through 'כי תשא'.

30:12.headline: Why counting heads could bring a plague
30:12.body: Rashi says a head count gives the evil eye power, and a plague follows, as happened when David counted Israel. So each person gives a coin and the coins are counted instead.

sources.quote: שֶׁהַמִּנְיָן שׁוֹלֵט בּוֹ עַיִן הָרָע, וְהַדֶּבֶר בָּא עֲלֵיהֶם, כְּמוֹ שֶׁמָּצִינוּ בִימֵי דָּוִד
sources.says: Rashi says the evil eye has power over a count, and pestilence comes on them, as in the days of David.

sources.quote: אַל תִּמְנֵם לַגֻּלְגֹּלֶת, אֶלָּא יִתְּנוּ כָּל אֶחָד מַחֲצִית הַשֶּׁקֶל וְתִמְנֶה אֶת הַשְּׁקָלִים וְתֵדַע מִנְיָנָם
sources.says: Rashi says not to count them by heads: each gives a half shekel, and you count the coins to learn their number.

30:13.headline: 'This is what they give': God showed Moses a coin of fire
30:13.body: The verse begins with זה, 'this', as if pointing at something. Rashi says God showed Moses a coin made of fire, weighing half a shekel, and said: like this they shall give.

sources.quote: הֶרְאָה לוֹ כְּמִין מַטְבֵּעַ שֶׁל אֵשׁ וּמִשְׁקָלָהּ מַחֲצִית הַשֶּׁקֶל וְאוֹמֵר לוֹ כָּזֶה יִתְּנוּ
sources.says: Rashi says God showed him a kind of coin of fire weighing half a shekel and told him: like this they shall give.

30:13.headline: 'Everyone who passes over': past the counter, or over God's commands
30:13.body: Rashi says the people were passed one by one in front of the counter, like sheep under a shepherd's hand. Kli Yakar hears another sense: these are the ones who 'passed over', that is broke, God's commands with the golden calf, and so need this atonement.

sources.quote: דֶּרֶךְ הַמּוֹנִין מַעֲבִירִין אֶת הַנִּמְנִין זֶה אַחַר זֶה, וְכֵן כֹּל אֲשֶׁר יַעֲבֹר תַּחַת הַשָּׁבֶט
sources.says: Rashi says those who count pass the counted ones by one after another, as in 'whatever passes under the rod'.

sources.quote: שֶׁהָיָה זֶה כֹּפֶר נֶפֶשׁ עַל עֲוֹן הָעֵגֶל, כִּי שָׁם עָבְרוּ יִשְׂרָאֵל עַל פִּקּוּדֵי ה׳ יְשָׁרִים אֲשֶׁר פָּקַד ה׳ לְמֹשֶׁה
sources.says: Kli Yakar says this was atonement for the golden calf, where Israel passed over the upright commands God gave Moses.

30:13.headline: Half a shekel for a sin done at half the day
30:13.body: Bahya cites a midrash: the people made the golden calf at midday, so they give half a shekel. Kli Yakar adds that the calf caused the tablets to break in two, so they give a coin split in two.

sources.quote: מחצית השקל לפי שחטאו במחצית היום לפיכך יתנו מחצית השקל
sources.says: Bahya cites a midrash: a half shekel, because they sinned at the half of the day.

sources.quote: לְפִי שֶׁבְּמַעֲשֵׂה הָעֵגֶל גָּרְמוּ שְׁבִירַת הַלּוּחוֹת לִשְׁנַיִם, עַל כֵּן יִתְּנוּ בֶּקַע, דְּהַיְנוּ שֶׁקֶל בָּקוּעַ לִשְׁנַיִם
sources.says: Kli Yakar says the calf caused the tablets to be broken in two, so they give a shekel split in two.

30:13.headline: A gerah: a tiny coin, or a carob seed?
30:13.body: Rashi says a גרה is a small coin, the same word as אגורת כסף, a piece of silver, in the book of Samuel. Ibn Ezra says the gerahs are carob seeds.

sources.quote: גרה. לְשׁוֹן מָעָה; וְכֵן בִּשְׁמְוּאֵל (א' ב'), יָבוֹא לְהִשְׁתַּחֲוֹת לוֹ לַאֲגוֹרַת כֶּסֶף
sources.says: Rashi says גרה means a ma'ah, a small coin, as in 'a piece of silver' in 1 Samuel 2.

sources.quote: ואלה הגרות גרגרות חרוב הם
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says these gerahs are carob seeds.

30:23.headline: Myrrh, or musk from a gazelle?
30:23.body: Ibn Ezra calls the word מר hard. Saadia Gaon translated it as musk, which does not come from trees, and the traders who bring it say it forms in a gazelle's throat.

sources.quote: ומלת מר קשה, והגאון תרגמה מוש"ק והנה איננו מעצים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word מר is hard; the Gaon translated it 'musk', which is not from trees.

sources.quote: ואומרים המביאים אותו כי הוא נעשה בגרון הצבי
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says those who bring it say it is formed in the throat of the gazelle.

30:31.headline: The word 'this' adds up to twelve measures of oil
30:31.body: The letters of זה, 'this', add up to twelve: ז is 7 and ה is 5. Rashi says this hints at the twelve logs of anointing oil.

sources.quote: זה. בְּגִימַטְרִיָּא תְּרֵיסַר לֻגִּין הֲווּ
sources.says: Rashi says זה in numbers equals twelve: there were twelve logs.

sources.quote: שמן משחת קדש יהיה זה לי, ז"ה בגימטריא תריסר לוגי
sources.says: Bahya says the same: the letters of זה add up to twelve logs.

30:34.headline: A bad-smelling spice in the incense, like sinners in prayer
30:34.body: Galbanum, חלבנה, smells bad, yet it is one of the incense spices. Rashi says this teaches us to include the sinners of Israel with us when we fast and pray.

sources.quote: בֹּשֶׂם שֶׁרֵיחוֹ רַע
sources.says: Rashi says galbanum is a spice with a bad smell.

sources.quote: לְלַמְּדֵנוּ שֶׁלֹּא יֵקַל בְּעֵינֵינוּ לְצָרֵף עִמָּנוּ בַּאֲגֻדַּת תַּעֲנִיּוֹתֵינוּ וּתְפִלּוֹתֵנוּ אֶת פּוֹשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁיִּהְיוּ נִמְנִין עִמָּנוּ
sources.says: Rashi says it teaches that we should not think little of joining the sinners of Israel to our fasts and prayers, counted with us.

sources.quote: מָנָה הַחֶלְבְּנָה בֵּין סַמְמָנֵי הַקְּטֹרֶת לְלַמֵּד אוֹתָנוּ לְצָרֵף פּוֹשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּכָל תַּעֲנִית
sources.says: Kli Yakar says galbanum is listed among the incense spices to teach us to include the sinners of Israel in every fast.

30:35.headline: 'Salted' incense: real salt, or stirred like sailors stir the sea
30:35.body: Ramban says ממלח means the incense had Sodom salt in it. Rashi follows Onkelos, 'well mixed', and links it to מלחים, sailors, who churn the water with their oars.

sources.quote: שֶׁיְּהֵא מָלוּחַ בְּמֶלַח סְדוֹמִית, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (כריתות ו.) מֶלַח סְדוֹמִית רֹבַע
sources.says: Ramban says it was salted with Sodom salt, as the sages say: a quarter-measure of Sodom salt.

sources.quote: וְאוֹמֵר אֲנִי שֶׁדּוֹמֶה לוֹ וַיִּירְאוּ הַמַּלָּחִים (יונה א'), מַלָּחַיִךְ וְחֹבְלָיִךְ (יחזקאל כ"ז) – עַל שֵׁם שֶׁמְּהַפְּכִין אֶת הַמַּיִם בִּמְשׁוֹטוֹת כְּשֶׁמַּנְהִיגִים אֶת הַסְּפִינָה
sources.says: Rashi says the word is like 'the sailors were afraid' in Jonah, since sailors stir the water with oars as they steer the ship.

31:2.headline: Betzalel: 'in the shadow of God'
31:2.body: The Talmud says Betzalel was named for his wisdom. Moses gave God's instructions in the wrong order, and Betzalel caught it. Moses said: were you in the shadow of God, בצל אל, that you knew?

sources.quote: בצלאל על שם חכמתו נקרא
sources.says: The Talmud says Betzalel was named for his wisdom.

sources.quote: שמא בצל אל היית וידעת
sources.says: Moses asks him: were you perhaps in the shadow of God, and so you knew?

31:3.headline: Three kinds of knowing: learned, worked out, and given
31:3.body: The verse lists חכמה, תבונה and דעת. Rashi tells them apart. חכמה is what you learn from others. תבונה is what you work out yourself from what you learned. דעת here is a gift from heaven.

sources.quote: מה שאדם שומע מאחרים ולמד
sources.says: Rashi says wisdom is what a person hears from others and learns.

sources.quote: מבין דבר מלבו מתוך דברים שלמד
sources.says: Rashi says understanding is grasping a thing on one's own from what one learned.

sources.quote: דעת. רוח הקדש
sources.says: Rashi says knowledge here means the holy spirit.

31:10.headline: A puzzling word: garments of service, of open weave, or of leftovers?
31:10.body: Rashi says שרד has no match in the Bible. Some read it as service, but he thinks it is Aramaic for cloth full of small holes. Ibn Ezra and Chizkuni tie it to שריד, a remnant, as if the covers were made from leftover cloth.

sources.quote: יש מפרשים לשון עבודה ושרות, כתרגומו לבושי שמושא, ואין לו דמיון במקרא
sources.says: Rashi says some explain it as service, as the Targum does, but it has no parallel in Scripture.

sources.quote: ואני אומר שהוא לשון ארמי
sources.says: Rashi says he thinks it is an Aramaic word for cloth with many small holes.

sources.quote: והנה מלת שרד מגזרת פליט ושריד
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word comes from 'survivor and remnant'.

sources.quote: לשון פליט ושריד מה שנשאר ממלאכת יריעות המשכן
sources.says: Chizkuni says it means what was left over from the cloth of the Tabernacle.

31:13.headline: 'Only' keep my Sabbaths: what does the 'only' leave out?
31:13.body: The sages read אך as a word that limits. Rashi says it limits the building work: even the Tabernacle may not be built on Shabbat. Ramban disagrees. He says it limits Shabbat itself, so that saving a life or a circumcision may override it.

sources.quote: כל אכין ורקין מעוטין – למעט שבת ממלאכת המשכן
sources.says: Rashi says every אך and רק limits, here to take Shabbat out of the Tabernacle work.

sources.quote: אבל המעוט הזה למילה או לפקוח נפש וכיוצא בהן שהן דוחין את השבת
sources.says: Ramban says the limit is for circumcision or saving a life, which override Shabbat.

31:15.headline: Not a short break, but full rest
31:15.body: Rashi says שבתון means settled rest, not a passing pause. Sforno adds that it forbids even things that are not formal work, so the day is free for higher things.

sources.quote: מנוחת מרגוע ולא מנוחת עראי
sources.says: Rashi says it is a rest of calm, not a temporary rest.

sources.quote: הנה נאסר בה אפלו דבר שאינו מכלל המלאכות
sources.says: Sforno says even something that is not one of the forms of work is forbidden on it.

31:17.headline: God 'caught His breath'? The Torah speaks our language
31:17.body: וינפש comes from נפש, breath or soul, and sounds like resting after effort. Rashi and Ibn Ezra say God never tires, so the word is put in human terms. Maimonides reads נפש as will: on the seventh day God's will was complete.

sources.quote: שמשיב נפשו ונשימתו בהרגיעו מטרח המלאכה
sources.says: Rashi says the word means getting back one's breath after the effort of work.

sources.quote: לשבר האזן מה שהיא יכולה לשמע
sources.says: Rashi says it is said to let the ear hear what it can take in.

sources.quote: והתורה דברה כלשון בני אדם להבין השומעים ואמר וינפש
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the Torah spoke in human language so listeners would understand, and said וינפש.

sources.quote: ואם כן משמעותו: השלמת רצונו וביצוע כל חפצו
sources.says: Maimonides says it means the completion of His will and the doing of all He wished.

31:18.headline: 'Written by the finger of God' means by God's will
31:18.body: God has no body. Maimonides says 'finger of God' is like 'the work of Your fingers' said of the heavens, which were made by God's word. So the writing came from God's will, not from a tool. Ibn Ezra also says it is said in human terms.

sources.quote: ודבריו "באצבע אלהים" הם כמו שנאמר על השמים "מעשה אצבעתיך"
sources.says: Maimonides says 'by the finger of God' is like 'the work of Your fingers' said about the heavens.

sources.quote: שווים לדבריו "כתובים בדבר אלהים"
sources.says: Maimonides says it equals 'written by the word of God'.

sources.quote: ודבר הכתוב באצבע אלהים על מנהג האדם
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the verse speaks of God's finger in the manner of people.

32:1.headline: 'Moses was late', or, the midrash says, 'six hours came'
32:1.body: בשש means delayed, as Onkelos translates. The midrash splits it into בא שש, 'six came'. Moses had said he would return within six hours of the fortieth day, and when six hours passed without him, the people turned to Aaron.

sources.quote: כי בשש משה. כתרגומו, לשון אחור
sources.says: Rashi says בשש means late, as Onkelos translates it.

sources.quote: אמר להם לסוף ארבעים יום אני בא בתוך שש שעות
sources.says: Rashi says Moses told them he would come at the end of forty days, within six hours.

sources.quote: מהו כי בשש, באו שש שעות ולא ירד
sources.says: The midrash reads בשש as 'six hours came and he did not come down'.

32:1.headline: 'Make us gods', or 'make us a leader'?
32:1.body: אלהים usually means God or gods. Bekhor Shor says here it means a judge and leader, as when Moses is made 'אלהים to Pharaoh'. The people wanted someone to stand in for Moses, not a new god, says Rabbeinu Bahya.

sources.quote: שופט דיין ומנהיג ודבר כמו נתתיך אלהים לפרעה
sources.says: Bekhor Shor says אלהים here means a judge, ruler and spokesman, as in 'I have made you a god to Pharaoh'.

sources.quote: שהם לא בקשוהו לאלוה כי אם למנהיג
sources.says: Rabbeinu Bahya says they did not ask for it as a god but as a leader.

32:4.headline: Did Aaron tie the gold in a cloth, or shape it with a tool?
32:4.body: Rashi gives two readings. ויצר may mean 'he tied', and חרט a cloth bag. Or ויצר means 'he shaped', and חרט is an engraver's tool, like a scribe's pen.

sources.quote: יש לתרגמו בשני פנים, האחד ויצר – לשון קשירה, בחרט – לשון סודר
sources.says: Rashi says it can be read two ways; first, 'he tied it' in a cloth.

sources.quote: והשני ויצר – לשון צורה, בחרט – כלי אמנות הצורפין
sources.says: Rashi's second reading: 'he shaped it' with a goldsmith's tool.

sources.quote: ומלת בחרט כמו דמות
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says בחרט means a likeness or form.

32:4.headline: 'These are your gods', not 'our gods': who was speaking?
32:4.body: The crowd says 'these are your gods, Israel', not 'our gods'. Rashi learns that the mixed crowd who left Egypt with Israel made the calf and then led Israel after it. Rabbeinu Bahya adds that the plural 'these' shows they wanted many gods.

sources.quote: ולא נאמר אלה אלהינו, מכאן שערב רב שעלו ממצרים הם שנקהלו על אהרן
sources.says: Rashi says it does not say 'our gods', which shows the mixed multitude gathered against Aaron.

sources.quote: ודקדקו זה מלשון אלה שהוא לשון רבים
sources.says: Rabbeinu Bahya says the sages learned it from the word 'these', which is plural.

32:5.headline: 'He built an altar' reread as 'he understood from the slain one'
32:5.body: The midrash reads ויבן as 'he understood' and מזבח as מזבוח, 'from the one slaughtered'. Aaron saw that Hur, who had rebuked the people, had been killed, and gave way to keep them from worse.

sources.quote: ראה חור בן אחותו שהיה מוכיחם והרגוהו, וזהו ויבן מזבח לפניו – ויבן מזבוח לפניו
sources.says: Rashi says Aaron saw that they had killed Hur for rebuking them, and reads it 'he understood from the slain one before him'.

sources.quote: ויבן מזבח לפניו. התבונן מן הזבוח לפניו
sources.says: Rabbeinu Bahya says it means he understood from the slain one before him.

32:6.headline: 'They rose to play': revelry, or something worse?
32:6.body: לצחק can mean to laugh or make merry. Rashi notes that elsewhere the same word hints at sexual sin and at bloodshed, and says both happened here. Ibn Ezra reads it more plainly as singing.

sources.quote: יש במשמע הזה גלוי עריות, כמו שנ' לצחק בי (בראשית ל"ט), ושפיכות דמים
sources.says: Rashi says the word implies sexual sin, as in Genesis 39, and bloodshed.

sources.quote: קול ענות. כמו נגינות וזהו ויקומו לצחק
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the sound was like songs, and that is what 'they rose to play' means.

32:7.headline: 'Go down': from the mountain, and from your greatness
32:7.body: רד means go down the mountain. Rashi reads it also as 'step down from your greatness'. God had given Moses his high place only for the people's sake.

sources.quote: מגדלתך – לא נתתי לך גדלה אלא בשבילם
sources.says: Rashi says it means go down from your greatness, since God gave it to Moses only for them.

sources.quote: לא בשביל כבודך אתה עולה לכאן אלא בשביל כבוד בני
sources.says: The midrash says Moses went up not for his own honor but for the honor of God's children.

32:7.headline: 'Your people': God and Moses each call Israel the other's
32:7.body: God tells Moses 'your people have sinned', not 'the people'. Rashi says God meant the mixed crowd Moses had taken in on his own. In verse 11 Moses answers 'your people, whom you brought out', and Rashbam reads it as: yours, not mine.

sources.quote: שחת העם לא נאמר, אלא עמך – ערב רב שקבלת מעצמך
sources.says: Rashi says it does not say 'the people' but 'your people': the mixed multitude Moses accepted on his own.

sources.quote: עמך אשר הוצאת - עמך ולא עמי
sources.says: Rashbam says Moses answers: they are your people, not mine.

32:10.headline: 'Leave me alone': God opens a door for Moses to pray
32:10.body: God says 'let me be', but Moses has not yet said a word for Israel. Rashi says God was hinting that it depended on Moses: if he prayed for them, God would not destroy them.

sources.quote: עדין לא שמענו שהתפלל משה עליהם והוא אומר הניחה לי
sources.says: Rashi notes that Moses had not yet prayed for them, and still God says 'leave me alone'.

sources.quote: אלא כאן פתח לו פתח והודיעו שהדבר תלוי בו
sources.says: Rashi says God opened a door for Moses and told him the matter depended on him.

32:11.headline: ויחל: Moses pleaded, fell sick, or undid God's vow
32:11.body: Onkelos reads ויחל simply as 'he prayed'. The midrash tries several roots. Moses fell sick (חלה) over the sin, or brought God a kind of gift, or 'released' God's own vow the way a vow is annulled.

sources.quote: וצלי משה קדם יי אלהיה
sources.says: Onkelos translates it 'Moses prayed before the Lord his God'.

sources.quote: רבי יהודה אומר, חלה משה כשעשו אותו מעשה. רבי נחמיה אומר, מהו ויחל משה, שהכניס לאלהים כמין דורון
sources.says: The midrash says Rabbi Yehuda read it as Moses fell ill, and Rabbi Nechemia as Moses brought God a kind of gift.

sources.quote: שהתיר נדרו של יוצרו
sources.says: Another view in the midrash says Moses released his Creator's vow.

32:13.headline: God swore 'by yourself', so the oath cannot run out
32:13.body: Moses reminds God that he swore to the fathers 'by yourself'. Rashi says God did not swear by heaven or earth, which will end, but by himself, who lasts forever. So the oath lasts too.

sources.quote: לא נשבעת להם בדבר שהוא כלה
sources.says: Rashi says God did not swear to them by something that comes to an end.

sources.quote: אלא בך, שאתה קים ושבועתך קימת לעולם
sources.says: Rashi says God swore by himself, since he endures and so his oath endures forever.

32:16.headline: Engraved (חרות) on the tablets, read as freedom (חירות)
32:16.body: חרות, engraved, appears only here, and Ibn Ezra says it has no partner word. Rashi says it is the same as חרט, carved. The midrash says not to read חרות but חירות, freedom: the tablets brought freedom from foreign kingdoms or from the angel of death.

sources.quote: והנכון שאין חבר לו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the right view is that the word has no partner in the Bible.

sources.quote: לשון חרת וחרט אחד הוא, שניהם לשון חקוק
sources.says: Rashi says חרת and חרט are one word, both meaning carved.

sources.quote: חרות אל תיקרי חרות אלא חירות
sources.says: Da'at Zekenim cites the teaching: do not read 'engraved' but 'freedom'.

sources.quote: רבי יהודה אמר: חרות מן המלכיות. ורבי נחמיה אמר: חרות מן מלאך המות
sources.says: The midrash says it means freedom from foreign kingdoms, or freedom from the angel of death.

32:18.headline: 'The sound of ענות': curses, or singing?
32:18.body: Moses hears neither a victory cry nor a cry of defeat, but קול ענות. Rashi and the midrash say it was insults and curses that pain the hearer. Ibn Ezra says it was singing.

sources.quote: קול חרופין וגדופין, המענין את נפש שומען כשנאמרין לו
sources.says: Rashi says it was a sound of insults and curses that pain whoever hears them.

sources.quote: מהו קול ענות? קול חרופין וגדופין
sources.says: The midrash says the sound was insults and curses.

sources.quote: קול ענות. כמו נגינות
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means songs.

32:18.headline: A one-time word: the cry of the weak, or of defeating?
32:18.body: חלושה appears only here. Rashi reads it as the cry of the weak who are losing. Rashbam ties it to ויחלש יהושע, 'Joshua weakened Amalek', and reads it as the shout of a win.

sources.quote: ולא קול חלשים שצועקים "וי אנוסה"
sources.says: Rashi says it is not the sound of the weak crying 'woe, let us flee'.

sources.quote: חלושה - נצחון, כדכתיב: ויחלוש יהושע
sources.says: Rashbam says חלושה means victory, as in 'Joshua weakened' Amalek.

32:20.headline: Moses made them drink: a test, or just a way to destroy the calf?
32:20.body: Moses grinds the calf, scatters it on the water, and has Israel drink. Rashi says he meant to test them, like the drinking test for a suspected wife. Chizkuni says plainly he only meant to scatter the gold, and they drank because it was in their water.

sources.quote: נתכון לבדקן כסוטות
sources.says: Rashi says Moses meant to test them like the suspected wife.

sources.quote: לפי הפשט לא נתכון להשקותן אלא לפזר זהב העגל ולבטלו מן העולם
sources.says: Chizkuni says by the plain sense he did not mean to make them drink, only to scatter the calf's gold and wipe it out.

32:25.headline: פרע: their shame laid bare, or the people let loose?
32:25.body: Rashi reads פרע as 'uncovered': their shame was exposed, the way a woman's hair is uncovered. Onkelos and Rashbam read it as 'idle, cut loose': they had dropped God's commandments.

sources.quote: פרע. מגלה; נתגלה שמצו וקלונו
sources.says: Rashi says פרע means uncovered: their disgrace was exposed.

sources.quote: ארי בטיל הוא ארי בטילנון אהרן
sources.says: Onkelos translates it 'that they were idle, for Aaron had made them idle'.

sources.quote: בטל מן המצות, ממצות בוראו
sources.says: Rashbam says it means they had stopped keeping their Creator's commandments.

32:29.headline: 'Fill your hands': a command, or 'you have already done it'?
32:29.body: Moses tells the Levites 'fill your hands today'. Rashi reads it as a command: through this act they are installed as priests. Rashbam and Chizkuni read it as past: you have already filled your hands, since you have already acted.

sources.quote: בדבר זה תתחנכו להיות כהנים למקום
sources.says: Rashi says by this deed they will be installed as priests to God.

sources.quote: מלאו ידכם היום - כמו: כי מלאו אחרי ה' - לשעבר
sources.says: Rashbam says מלאו here is past tense, as in 'they followed God fully'.

sources.quote: ואין לומר מלאו ידיכם להבא שהרי כבר עשו כדברי משה
sources.says: Chizkuni says it cannot mean the future, since they had already done what Moses said.

32:32.headline: 'Erase me from your book': the Torah, or the book of life?
32:32.body: Moses asks to be erased from God's book. Rashi says it means the whole Torah. Rashbam says the book of life. A midrash in Rabbeinu Bahya notes that Moses' name is indeed missing from one Torah portion, Tetzaveh.

sources.quote: מכל התורה כלה
sources.says: Rashi says it means erase me from the whole Torah.

sources.quote: ספר חיים אשר כתבת
sources.says: Rashbam says it is the book of life that God wrote.

sources.quote: נמחה שמו מפרשת ואתה תצוה שלא נזכר שם שמו של משה כלל
sources.says: Rabbeinu Bahya cites a midrash that Moses' name was erased from the portion Tetzaveh, where it never appears.

33:11.headline: 'Face to face', though no one can see God's face
33:11.body: Later in the chapter God says no one can see his face. Maimonides says 'face to face' here means presence to presence, with no go-between. Onkelos translates it 'speech with speech'.

sources.ref: Guide for the Perplexed, Part 1, Chapter 37:3
sources.quote: כלומר נוכחות בנוכחות, בלי תיווך
sources.says: Maimonides says 'face to face' means presence to presence, without a go-between.

sources.quote: מַמְלַל עִם מַמְלַל
sources.says: Onkelos translates 'face to face' as 'speech with speech'.

33:14.headline: 'My face will go': God himself, or God's anger?
33:14.body: Rashi follows Onkelos: no more angel, I myself will go with you. Maimonides lists this verse among those where פנים means anger.

sources.quote: לֹא אֶשְׁלַח עוֹד מַלְאָךְ, אֲנִי בְעַצְמִי אֵלֵךְ
sources.says: Rashi says God will no longer send an angel but will go himself.

sources.quote: שְׁכִנְתִּי תְהַךְ וְאָנִיחַ לָךְ
sources.says: Onkelos translates: my presence will go, and I will give you rest.

sources.ref: Guide for the Perplexed, Part 1, Chapter 37:2
sources.quote: במשמעות הזו משתמשים בו רבות במובן של כעס ה' ורוגזו
sources.says: Maimonides says פנים is often used to mean God's anger.

sources.ref: Guide for the Perplexed, Part 1, Chapter 37:2
sources.quote: פָּנַי יֵלֵכוּ וַהֲנִחֹתִי לָךְ
sources.says: Maimonides gives this verse as one of his examples of that sense.

33:21.headline: 'A place with me': a spot on the mountain, or more?
33:21.body: Rashi's plain reading is a spot on the mountain where God would hide Moses. His midrash says God is the place of the world, and the world is not his place. Maimonides reads 'place' as a level of thought, not of eyesight.

sources.quote: יֵשׁ מָקוֹם מוּכָן לִי לְצָרְכְּךָ שֶׁאַטְמִינְךָ שָׁם שֶׁלֹּא תִזֹּק
sources.says: Rashi says there is a place ready where God will hide Moses so he is not harmed.

sources.quote: שֶׁהַקָּבָּ"ה מְקוֹמוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם וְאֵין עוֹלָמוֹ מְקוֹמוֹ
sources.says: Rashi brings the midrash: God is the place of the world, and the world is not his place.

sources.ref: Guide for the Perplexed, Part 1, Chapter 8:3
sources.quote: דרגת עיון והתבוננות השכל, לא התבוננות העין
sources.says: Maimonides says 'place' here means a level of thought and reflection, not looking with the eye.

33:23.headline: Moses sees God's 'back': what was it?
33:23.body: Rashi says God showed Moses the knot of the tefillin. Maimonides says 'my back' means what follows from God: everything he made.

sources.quote: הֶרְאָהוּ קֶשֶׁר שֶׁל תְּפִלִּין
sources.says: Rashi says God showed him the knot of the tefillin.

sources.ref: Guide for the Perplexed, Part 1, Chapter 38:2
sources.quote: תשיג מה שהלך אחריי והידמה לי ונבע מרצוני, כלומר את כל ברואיו
sources.says: Maimonides says Moses would grasp what follows from God and comes from his will, that is, all his creatures.

34:1.headline: 'Carve for yourself': the midrash says the chips were Moses' to keep
34:1.body: God tells Moses פסל לך, 'carve for yourself' two tablets. Rashi brings a midrash that hears פסולת, 'chips', in the word: God showed Moses a sapphire quarry and said the chips were his, and Moses grew rich from them.

sources.quote: הֶרְאָהוּ מַחְצַב סַנְפִּירִינוֹן מִתּוֹךְ אָהֳלוֹ וְאָמַר לוֹ הַפְּסֹלֶת יִהְיֶה שֶׁלְּךָ; מִשָּׁם נִתְעַשֵּׁר מֹשֶׁה הַרְבֵּה
sources.says: Rashi says God showed Moses a sapphire quarry in his tent and told him the chips would be his, and from them Moses became very rich.

sources.quote: ואמר לו הקב"ה פסל לך הפסולת שלך
sources.says: Rabbeinu Bahya cites the midrash that God told Moses: carve for yourself, the chips are yours.

34:6.headline: 'El' here is a name of mercy, Rashi says, not of power
34:6.body: אל often means 'the Strong One', and Ibn Ezra reads it that way here. Rashi, citing the Mekhilta, says it too is mercy, as in 'Eli, Eli, why have You forsaken me', a cry no one makes to strict justice.

sources.quote: אַף זוֹ מִדַּת רַחֲמִים, וְכֵן הוּא אוֹמֵר אֵלִי אֵלִי לָמָה עֲזַבְתָּנִי
sources.says: Rashi says El is also a name of mercy, as in 'my God, my God, why have You forsaken me'.

sources.quote: וְאֵין לוֹמַר לְמִדַּת הַדִּין לָמָה עֲזַבְתָּנִי
sources.says: Rashi adds that one would not say 'why have You forsaken me' to the attribute of justice.

sources.quote: ואל. כמו תקיף שיעשה הנכון בחכמה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says El means strong, one who does what is right with wisdom.

34:7.headline: Notzer: God keeps kindness, or makes it sprout
34:7.body: נצר usually means 'keeps' or 'guards'. Ramban offers a second reading, 'makes it grow', from נצר, a young shoot, as in 'a shoot from his roots will bear fruit' (Isaiah 11:1).

sources.quote: אוֹ נוֹצֵר, מַצְמִיחַ, מִן "וְנֵצֶר מִשָּׁרָשָׁיו יִפְרֶה"
sources.says: Ramban says נוצר may mean 'makes sprout', from 'a shoot (נצר) from his roots will bear fruit'.

34:7.headline: 'He clears, He will not clear': one doubled verb, three readings
34:7.body: Rashi's plain reading: God does not let sin go entirely but collects a little at a time; the rabbis split the words: He clears those who repent, not those who do not. Maimonides reads it as 'He will not wipe them out completely'.

sources.quote: שֶׁאֵינוֹ מְוַתֵּר עַל הֶעָוֹן לְגַמְרֵי, אֶלָּא נִפְרָע מִמֶּנּוּ מְעַט מְעַט
sources.says: Rashi says by the plain sense God does not forgo the sin entirely but exacts it little by little.

sources.quote: מְנַקֶּה הוּא לַשָּׁבִים וְלֹא יְנַקֶּה לְשֶׁאֵינָן שָׁבִים
sources.says: Rashi says the rabbis read it: He clears those who repent and does not clear those who do not.

sources.quote: פירושם 'וְשָׁרֵשׁ לא ישרש' (=לא ישמיד לגמרי)
sources.says: Maimonides says the words mean 'He will not uproot', that is, not destroy completely.

34:7.headline: Four generations against two thousand: good outweighs punishment 500 to 1
34:7.body: Rashi reads רבעים as the fourth generation. He sets it against 'kindness for thousands', which he takes as two thousand generations, and finds that reward outweighs punishment five hundred to one.

sources.quote: נִמְצֵאת מִדָּה טוֹבָה מְרֻבָּה עַל מִדַּת פֻּרְעָנוּת אַחַת לַחֲמֵשׁ מֵאוֹת
sources.says: Rashi says the measure of good is greater than the measure of punishment, one to five hundred.

sources.quote: לִשְׁנֵי אֲלָפִים דּוֹרוֹת
sources.says: Rashi says 'for thousands' means for two thousand generations.

34:8.headline: Vayikod: Moses bowed until the crown of his head met the ground
34:8.body: Ibn Ezra traces ויקד to קדקד, the crown of the head. Moses bent so low that he put the top of his head on the earth.

sources.quote: מבעלי הכפל מגזרת קדקד ששם קדקדו בארץ
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word comes from קדקד, the crown of the head, because he put his crown on the ground.

34:9.headline: 'For they are stiff-necked': Moses turns God's reason into a plea
34:9.body: God had refused to go among the people because they were stiff-necked, and here Moses asks Him to go כי they are. Rashi reads כי as 'if', Ibn Ezra cites a reading 'although', and Ramban keeps 'because': God will be kinder to such a people than an angel.

sources.quote: לֹא אֶעֱלֶה בְּקִרְבְּךָ כִּי עַם קְשֵׁה עֹרֶף
sources.says: Or HaChaim notes that God earlier said He would not go among them because they were stiff-necked.

sources.quote: וְאִם עַם קְשֵׁה עֹרֶף הוּא וְיַמְרוּ בְךָ
sources.says: Rashi reads it: and if they are stiff-necked and rebel against You, You will forgive.

sources.quote: יֵשׁ כִּי בִּמְקוֹם אִם
sources.says: Rashi says כי sometimes stands for 'if'.

sources.quote: על דעת רבי מרינוס אעפ"י שעם קשה עורף הוא
sources.says: Ibn Ezra cites Rabbi Marinus, who reads it as 'even though they are a stiff-necked people'.

sources.quote: שֶׁיֵּלֵךְ בְּקִרְבָּם בַּעֲבוּר שֶׁהֵם עַם קְשֵׁה עֹרֶף
sources.says: Ramban keeps the plain sense: God should go among them because they are stiff-necked.

sources.quote: יִהְיֶה ה' טוֹב לִקְשִׁי עָרְפָּם יוֹתֵר מִמַּלְאָךְ
sources.says: Ramban says God will be better for their stubbornness than an angel would be.

34:9.headline: 'Take us as Your inheritance', not 'give us our land'
34:9.body: ונחלתנו could mean 'give us an inheritance'. Rashi and Rabbeinu Bahya read it the other way round: make us Your own special possession.

sources.quote: וְתִתְּנֵנוּ לְךָ לְנַחֲלָה מְיֻחֶדֶת
sources.says: Rashi says it means: give us to Yourself as a special inheritance.

sources.quote: ואמר ונחלתנו והיה לו לומר ותנחילנו, אבל באורו שתנחיל אותנו שאנחנו נהיה נחלה שלך
sources.says: Rabbeinu Bahya says Moses would have said ותנחילנו for 'give us land'; ונחלתנו means we will be Your inheritance.

34:22.headline: Tekufah: the point where the year comes round again
34:22.body: Rashi says תקופה means going round, a circuit: the festival falls as the year turns to the start of the next. Ibn Ezra ties it to the sun entering Libra close to Yom Kippur.

sources.quote: לְשׁוֹן מְסִבָּה וְהַקָּפָה
sources.says: Rashi says תקופה means turning around and going round.

sources.quote: שֶׁהִיא בַחֲזָרַת הַשָּׁנָה – בִּתְחִלַּת הַשָּׁנָה הַבָּאָה
sources.says: Rashi says it is at the year's return, at the start of the coming year.

sources.quote: כי השמש תכנס במזל המאזנים סמוך ליום העשור
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the sun enters Libra near Yom Kippur.

34:29.headline: Karan: Moses' face sent out rays, not horns
34:29.body: קרן is the word for a horn. Rashi says light shone out of Moses' face in beams like horns, Rashbam calls the 'ox horns' reading nonsense, and Onkelos renders 'the radiance of his face grew great'.

sources.quote: לְשׁוֹן קַרְנַיִם, שֶׁהָאוֹר מַבְהִיק וּבוֹלֵט כְּמִין קֶרֶן
sources.says: Rashi says it comes from horns: the light shone and stood out like a horn.

sources.quote: והמדמהו לקרני ראם קרניו אינו אלא שטות
sources.says: Rashbam says comparing it to the horns of a wild ox is nonsense.

sources.quote: ומלת קרן. מגזרת קרנים מידו לו
sources.says: Ibn Ezra links it to 'rays from His hand' in Habakkuk 3:4.

sources.quote: אֲרֵי סְגֵי זִיו יְקָרָא דְאַפּוֹהִי
sources.says: Onkelos renders: that the radiance of the glory of his face had grown great.

35:1.headline: Moses gathered the people with words, not hands
35:1.body: ויקהל is a causative form: Moses "caused them to assemble". Rashi says he did not round people up by hand. They came together at his word.

sources.quote: וְהוּא לְשׁוֹן הִפְעִיל, שֶׁאֵינוֹ אוֹסֵף אֲנָשִׁים בְּיָּדַיִם, אֶלָּא הֵן נֶאֱסָפִין עַל פִּי דִּבּוּרוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says the verb is causative: Moses did not gather people with his hands, they gathered at his word.

35:13.headline: "Bread of faces": loaves with faces on both sides
35:13.body: The showbread is called לחם הפנים, "bread of the faces". Rashi says the name comes from its shape: each loaf had faces turned both ways, like an open box.

sources.quote: עַל שֵׁם שֶׁהָיוּ לוֹ פָּנִים לְכָאן וּלְכָאן, שֶׁהוּא עָשׂוּי כְּמִין תֵּבָה פְרוּצָה
sources.says: Rashi says it is named for having faces on this side and that, being made like an open box.

35:19.headline: Travel covers, or garments of service?
35:19.body: בגדי השרד is an unusual phrase. Rashi says these were cloths that covered the ark, table, lamp and altars when the camp traveled. Onkelos translates it as "garments of service" for the holy place.

sources.quote: לְכַסּוֹת הָאָרוֹן וְהַשֻּׁלְחָן, הַמְּנוֹרָה וְהַמִּזְבְּחוֹת בִּשְׁעַת סִלּוּק מַסָּעוֹת
sources.says: Rashi says they covered the ark, table, menorah and altars when the camp set out on its journeys.

sources.quote: לְבוּשֵׁי שִׁמּוּשָׁא לְשַׁמָּשָׁא בְקוּדְשָׁא
sources.says: Onkelos translates it as "garments of service, to serve in the holy place".

35:21.headline: Their hearts lifted them to crafts no one taught them
35:21.body: The verse speaks of everyone "whose heart lifted him". Ramban says these were the craftsmen: none had trained in these skills, but they found the ability in themselves and stepped forward.

sources.quote: כִּי לֹא הָיָה בָּהֶם שֶׁלָּמַד אֶת הַמְּלָאכוֹת הָאֵלֶּה מִמְּלַמֵּד, אוֹ מִי שֶׁאִמֵּן בָּהֶן יָדָיו כְּלָל, אֲבָל מָצָא בְּטִבְעוֹ שֶׁיֵּדַע לַעֲשׂוֹת כֵּן
sources.says: Ramban says none of them had learned these crafts from a teacher or practiced them, but each found in his nature that he knew how.

35:26.headline: The women spun the goat hair while it was still on the goats
35:26.body: The verse says the women "spun the goats", not "the goat hair". Rashi and the Talmud read it literally: they spun the hair right on the animals, a rare and special skill.

sources.quote: הִיא הָיְתָה אָמָּנוּת יְתֵרָה, שֶׁמֵּעַל גַּבֵּי הָעִזִּים טוֹוִין אוֹתָם
sources.says: Rashi says it was an extra skill: they spun the hair on the goats' backs.

sources.quote: וְטָווּי בָּעִזִּים, אַלְמָא טְוִויָּה עַל גַּבֵּי בְּהֵמָה שְׁמָהּ טְוִויָּה! חָכְמָה יְתֵירָה שָׁאנֵי
sources.says: The Talmud cites the teaching that they spun on the goats and answers that this was an exceptional skill.

35:27.headline: The princes came late, so their title lost a letter
35:27.body: The word for "princes" is spelled here without its usual yod. Rashi says the princes waited to give until others had given, and for that delay a letter was taken from their name.

sources.quote: וּלְפִי שֶׁנִּתְעַצְּלוּ מִתְּחִלָּה נֶחְסְרָה אוֹת מִשְּׁמָם, וְהַנְּשִׂאִם כְּתִיב
sources.says: Rashi says that because they were lazy at first, a letter is missing from their name, and it is written והנשאם.

35:30.headline: Bezalel: "in the shadow of God"
35:30.body: The midrash splits the builder's name into בצל אל, "in God's shade". He is the one who sits in God's shadow.

sources.quote: ולמה נקרא שמו בצלאל, שהוא יושב בצל אל
sources.says: The midrash says he was called Bezalel because he sits in the shadow of God.

35:31.headline: Bezalel's three gifts are the three God used to make the world
35:31.body: Bezalel is filled with wisdom, understanding and knowledge. The Talmud notes that Proverbs uses the same three words for how God founded heaven and earth. So, it says, Bezalel knew how to combine the letters that created the world.

sources.quote: יוֹדֵעַ הָיָה בְּצַלְאֵל לְצָרֵף אוֹתִיּוֹת שֶׁנִּבְרְאוּ בָּהֶן שָׁמַיִם וָאָרֶץ. כְּתִיב הָכָא: ״וַיְמַלֵּא אֹתוֹ רוּחַ אֱלֹהִים בְּחׇכְמָה וּבִתְבוּנָה וּבְדַעַת״, וּכְתִיב הָתָם: ״ה׳ בְּחׇכְמָה יָסַד אָרֶץ כּוֹנֵן שָׁמַיִם בִּתְבוּנָה״
sources.says: The Talmud says Bezalel knew how to combine the letters with which heaven and earth were created, and proves it from the shared words wisdom, understanding and knowledge.

35:34.headline: A partner from the lowest tribe, set beside the highest
35:34.body: Oholiab came from Dan, a tribe descended from a handmaid. Rashi says God made him equal to Bezalel of great Judah, to fulfill the verse "the noble is not favored over the poor".

sources.quote: מִשֵּׁבֶט דָּן מִן הַיְרוּדִין שֶׁבַּשְּׁבָטִים – מִבְּנֵי הַשְּׁפָחוֹת – וְהִשְׁוָהוּ הַמָּקוֹם לִבְצַלְאֵל לִמְלֶאכֶת הַמִּשְׁכָּן וְהוּא מִגְּדוֹלֵי הַשְּׁבָטִים, לְקַיֵּם מַה שֶּׁנֶּ' וְלֹא נִכַּר שׁוֹעַ לִפְנֵי דָל
sources.says: Rashi says Oholiab was from Dan, one of the lowest tribes, yet God made him equal to Bezalel of a great tribe, to fulfill "the noble is not favored over the poor".

36:6.headline: Moses' call became the source for not carrying on the Sabbath
36:6.body: The Talmud says Moses sat in the Levites' camp, a public area, and this call told people not to carry things out of their own tents into it. It links ויעבירו, 'they passed the word', to the same verb used for the shofar on Yom Kippur, a day when work is forbidden.

sources.quote: מֹשֶׁה הֵיכָן הֲוָה יָתֵיב? — בְּמַחֲנֵה לְוִיָּה, וּמַחֲנֵה לְוִיָּה רְשׁוּת הָרַבִּים הֲוַאי, וְקָאֲמַר לְהוּ לְיִשְׂרָאֵל: לָא תַּפִּיקוּ וְתַיְתוֹ מֵרְשׁוּת הַיָּחִיד דִּידְכוּ לִרְשׁוּת הָרַבִּים
sources.says: The Talmud says Moses was in the Levite camp, a public domain, and told Israel not to carry from their private domain into the public domain.

sources.quote: גָּמַר ״הַעֲבָרָה״ ״הַעֲבָרָה״ מִיּוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים
sources.says: The Talmud learns from the shared word 'passing' that this was on a day when carrying is forbidden, as on Yom Kippur.

sources.quote: מכאן אמרו רבותינו לאסור הוצאה בשבת מרשות לרשות
sources.says: Chizkuni says the sages learned from here that carrying from one domain to another is forbidden on the Sabbath.

36:7.headline: 'Enough' and 'too much' at once: how can both be true?
36:7.body: The verse says the gifts were 'enough' and also 'left over'. Or HaChaim says these contradict. He suggests that God, out of love for the givers, let every gift find a place in the Tabernacle, even more than it should have held.

sources.quote: הֵם שְׁנֵי דְּבָרִים הַפְכִּיִּים: אִם דַּיָּם אֵינוֹ הוֹתֵר, וְאִם הוֹתֵר אֵינוֹ דַּיָּם
sources.says: Or HaChaim says 'enough' and 'left over' are opposites: if it is enough it is not extra, and if extra it is not just enough.

sources.quote: לִכְבוֹד כָּל אִישׁ שֶׁטָּרְחוּ וְהֵבִיאוּ, וְנִכְנַס כָּל הַמּוּבָא בֵּית ה׳ בִּמְלֶאכֶת הַמִּשְׁכָּן
sources.says: Or HaChaim suggests God cared for the honor of everyone who took the trouble to give, so all that was brought went into the Tabernacle work.

36:20.headline: Boards that 'stand': upright, or standing forever?
36:20.body: Rashi says עמדים means the boards stood upright, not laid flat one on top of another. The Talmud adds other readings: they stood the way the trees grew, and they will stand for ever and ever.

sources.quote: שֶׁיְּהֵא אֹרֶךְ הַקְּרָשִׁים זָקוּף לְמַעְלָה בְּקִירוֹת הַמִּשְׁכָּן, וְלֹא תַעֲשֶׂה הַכְּתָלִים בִּקְרָשִׁים שׁוֹכְבִים, לִהְיוֹת רֹחַב הַקְּרָשִׁים לְגֹבַהּ הַכְּתָלִים קֶרֶשׁ עַל קֶרֶשׁ
sources.says: Rashi says the boards stood with their length upright, not lying one on another.

sources.quote: שֶׁעוֹמְדִים דֶּרֶךְ גְּדִילָתָן. דָּבָר אַחֵר: ״עוֹמְדִים״, שֶׁמַּעֲמִידִין אֶת צִפּוּיָין. דָּבָר אַחֵר: ״עוֹמְדִים״. שֶׁמָּא תֹּאמַר אָבַד סִבְרָן וּבָטֵל סִכּוּיָין — תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר: ״עוֹמְדִים״, שֶׁעוֹמְדִין לְעוֹלָם וּלְעוֹלָמִים
sources.says: The Talmud reads עומדים three ways: standing as they grew, holding up their gold plating, and standing for ever and ever.

36:22.headline: Pegs set apart like the rungs of a ladder
36:22.body: משלבת comes from שלב, a rung. Rashi says the two pegs at the foot of each board stood apart like the rungs of a ladder, their tips shaped to slide into the silver bases.

sources.quote: משלבת. עֲשׂוּיוֹת כְּמִין שְׁלִיבוֹת סֻלָּם, וּמֻבְדָּלוֹת זוֹ מִזּוֹ, וּמְשֻׁפִּין רָאשֵׁיהֶם לִכָּנֵס בְּתוֹךְ חֲלַל הָאֶדֶן כִּשְׁלִיבָה הַנִּכְנֶסֶת בְּנֶקֶב עַמּוּדֵי הַסֻּלָּם
sources.says: Rashi says they were made like the rungs of a ladder, set apart from each other, with tips shaped to go into the hollow of the base.

36:35.headline: The parochet: a screen between the king and the people
36:35.body: Rashi says פרכת means a partition. He compares the sages' word פרגוד, the curtain that separates a king from his people.

sources.quote: פרכת. לְשׁוֹן מְחִצָּה הוּא, וּבִלְשׁוֹן חֲכָמִים פַּרְגּוֹד דָּבָר הַמַּבְדִּיל בֵּין הַמֶּלֶךְ וּבֵין הָעָם
sources.says: Rashi says פרכת means a partition, called פרגוד by the sages: something that separates the king from the people.

36:35.headline: 'A designer's work': a different picture on each side
36:35.body: Rashi says מעשה חשב was woven as two layers, so the pictures on the two sides did not match. The Talmud says this was a weaver's work, and so it had two faces.

sources.quote: שֶׁזּוֹ הִיא אֲרִיגָה שֶׁל שְׁתֵּי קִירוֹת, וְהַצִּיּוּרִין שֶׁמִּשְּׁנֵי עֲבָרֶיהָ אֵינָן דּוֹמִין זֶה לָזֶה
sources.says: Rashi says this is weaving with two walls, and the pictures on its two sides are not alike.

sources.quote: חוֹשֵׁב״ — מַעֲשֵׂה אוֹרֵג, לְפִיכָךְ שְׁנֵי פַּרְצוּפוֹת
sources.says: The Talmud says חושב is a weaver's work, and so it has two faces.

36:37.headline: 'Embroiderer's work': the same picture on both sides
36:37.body: For the entrance screen the verse says מעשה רקם. Rashi says the pictures were sewn with a needle, the same on both sides. The Talmud agrees: needlework, so one face.

sources.quote: מעשה רקם. הַצּוּרוֹת עֲשׂוּיוֹת בּוֹ מַעֲשֵׂה מַחַט, כְּפַרְצוּף שֶׁל עֵבֶר זֶה כָּךְ פַּרְצוּף שֶׁל עֵבֶר זֶה
sources.says: Rashi says the figures were made with a needle, and each side shows the same face.

sources.quote: רוֹקֵם״ — מַעֲשֵׂה מַחַט, לְפִיכָךְ פַּרְצוּף אֶחָד
sources.says: The Talmud says רוקם is needlework, and so it has one face.

37:2.headline: A crown (zer) that can become a stranger (zar)
37:2.body: The gold rim around the top of the ark is a זר, a crown. Rashi says it stands for the crown of Torah. The Talmud plays on the word: if a person is worthy, it becomes his crown; if not, it becomes זרה, a stranger to him.

sources.quote: זר זהב. כְּמִין כֶּתֶר מֻקָּף לוֹ סָבִיב
sources.says: Rashi says the זר was like a crown circling the top of the ark.

sources.quote: וְהוּא סִימָן לְכֶתֶר תּוֹרָה
sources.says: Rashi says it is a sign of the crown of Torah.

sources.quote: שֶׁל אָרוֹן — עֲדַיִין מוּנָּח הוּא, כָּל הָרוֹצֶה לִיקַּח — יָבֹא וְיִקַּח
sources.says: The Talmud says the crown of the ark is still in its place, and anyone who wants it may come and take it.

sources.quote: זָכָה — נַעֲשֵׂית לוֹ זֵיר, לֹא זָכָה — זָרָה הֵימֶנּוּ
sources.says: The Talmud says: if he merits, it becomes a crown (זיר) for him; if not, it becomes a stranger (זרה) to him.

37:3.headline: The ark's four paamot: its corners, or its feet?
37:3.body: Rashi follows the Aramaic translation: פעמתיו are corners, and the rings sat at the top corners. Ibn Ezra says he searched all of Scripture and found פעם only as a foot, so the ark stood on feet and did not sit on the ground.

sources.quote: פעמותיו. כְּתַרְגוּמוֹ זִוְיָתֵיהּ
sources.says: Rashi says פעמותיו means its corners, as the Aramaic translation has it.

sources.quote: חפשתי בכל המקרא ולא מצאתי פעם שהוא זויות, רק מלשון רגל, רגלי עני פעמי דלים (ישעי' כו ו) וישם לדרך פעמיו (תה' פה יד) מה יפו פעמיך (ש"ה ז ב) ורבים ככה על כן הוצרכתי לפרש כי רגלים היו לארון
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says he never found פעם meaning a corner in Scripture, only a foot, and so the ark had feet.

sources.quote: ויש מפרשים פעמתיו רגלו
sources.says: Chizkuni brings both views, and notes that some explain פעמתיו as its feet.

37:6.headline: Kaporet: a lid, with a name close to atonement
37:6.body: Rashi and Rashbam say כפרת simply means the cover laid on the open ark. Ibn Ezra reports that Yefet tied it to לכפר, 'to atone', as sin being covered over; Ibn Ezra himself links that word to כופר, a ransom.

sources.quote: כפרת. כִּסּוּי עַל הָאָרוֹן
sources.says: Rashi says the כפרת is a cover on the ark, which was open at the top.

sources.quote: כפרת - ל' כיסוי
sources.says: Rashbam says כפרת is a word for covering.

sources.quote: ואמר יפת כי כמוהו לכפר עליו (ויקרא א ד) כמו כסוי חטאה (תה' לב א), ולפי דעתי שמלת לכפר עליו, מגזרת כופר
sources.says: Ibn Ezra reports Yefet's view that it is like 'to atone', as in covering a sin, and says he himself derives that word from כופר, ransom.

37:7.headline: Cherubs: 'like a child', or great winged birds?
37:7.body: The Talmud reads כרוב as 'like a child', since in Babylon a child was called רביא. Rashi follows this: they had a child's face. Rashbam says that by the plain sense they were great winged birds, as in Ezekiel.

sources.quote: וּמַאי כְּרוּב? אָמַר רַבִּי אֲבָהוּ: כְּרָבְיָא
sources.says: The Talmud says כרוב means 'like a child', for in Babylon they call a child רביא.

sources.quote: כרבים. דְּמוּת פַּרְצוּף תִּינוֹק לָהֶם
sources.says: Rashi says the cherubs had the face of a child.

sources.quote: כרבים - עופות, כדכתיב: (יחזקאל כח) את כרוב ממשח הסוכך. עוף גדול בעל כנפים. וחכמים פירשו: פני תינוק
sources.says: Rashbam says they were birds, a great bird with wings as in Ezekiel, and notes the sages said a child's face.

37:7.headline: Miksha: beaten out of one block of gold, not joined on
37:7.body: Rashi says the cherubs were not made apart and then attached. A lump of gold was hammered until they rose out of the lid itself. He ties the word to the Aramaic for knocking, as in Daniel's knees that 'knocked one against the other'.

sources.quote: שֶׁלֹּא תַעֲשֵׂם בִּפְנֵי עַצְמָם וּתְחַבְּרֵם בְּרָאשֵׁי הַכַּפֹּרֶת לְאַחַר עֲשִׂיָּתָם כְּמַעֲשֵׂה צוֹרְפִים שֶׁקּוֹרִין שולד"יר בְּלַעַז, אֶלָּא הַטֵּל זָהָב הַרְבֵּה בִּתְחִלַּת עֲשִׂיַּת הַכַּפֹּרֶת, וְהַכֵּה בְּפַטִּישׁ וּבְקֻרְנָס בָּאֶמְצַע
sources.says: Rashi says not to make them separately and attach them, but to put down a lot of gold and beat it with a hammer in the middle.

sources.quote: כְּמוֹ דָּא לְדָא נָקְשָׁן
sources.says: Rashi compares the word to Daniel's 'one knocked against the other'.

37:16.headline: Yusach: covered over, or poured out?
37:16.body: יסך looks like נסך, pouring a drink offering, and Onkelos translates it as pouring. Rashi says here it means covering, like סכך, a roof of branches: the rods lay over the loaves like a roof.

sources.quote: דִּי יִתְנַסַּךְ בְּהוֹן
sources.says: Onkelos renders it with the Aramaic word for being poured.

sources.quote: אשר יסך בהן. אֲשֶׁר יְכֻסֶּה בָהֵן, וְעַל קְשֹׂתָיו הוּא אוֹמֵר אֲשֶׁר יֻסַּךְ, שֶׁהָיוּ עָלָיו כְּמִין סְכָךְ וְכִסּוּי, וְכֵן בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר הוּא אוֹמֵר וְאֵת קְשׂוֹת הַנָּסֶךְ (במדבר ד'), וְזֶה וָזֶה, יֻסַּךְ וְהַנָּסֶךְ, לְשׁוֹן סְכָךְ וְכִסּוּי הֵם
sources.says: Rashi says יסך means covered: the rods were over the table like a roof, and both יסך and הנסך are words for covering.

sources.quote: ומלת נסך לטעמים רבים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word נסך is used in many senses.

37:16.headline: Kesot: hollow rods between the loaves, or jugs for water?
37:16.body: Rashi says they were like reeds split down the middle, laid between the loaves so air could pass and the bread would not go moldy. Chizkuni says they held the water poured on the flour to knead the bread.

sources.quote: הֵן כְּמִין חֲצָאֵי קָנִים חֲלוּלִים הַנִּסְדָּקִין לְאָרְכָּן (מנחות צ"ו), דֻּגְמָתָן עוֹשֶׂה שֶׁל זָהָב, וּמְסַדֵּר ג' עַל רֹאשׁ כָּל לֶחֶם, שֶׁיֵּשֵׁב לֶחֶם הָאַחֵר עַל גַּבֵּי אוֹתָן הַקָּנִים, וּמַבְדִּילִין בֵּין לֶחֶם לְלֶחֶם כְּדֵי שֶׁתִּכָּנֵס הָרוּחַ בֵּינֵיהֶם וְלֹא יִתְעַפְּשׁוּ
sources.says: Rashi says they were like hollow half-reeds set between the loaves so air could get in and the bread would not mold.

sources.quote: וקשותיו שנותנים בהם מים ללוש הלחם
sources.says: Chizkuni says they held water for kneading the bread.

37:16.headline: Menakiyot: props for the bread, or tools for cleaning?
37:16.body: Rashi follows the Aramaic translation: these were tall gold props that held up the stacked loaves. Chizkuni reads the word plainly, from נקה, 'clean': tools to clear the oven of ash and to wipe the table.

sources.quote: ומנקיתיו. תַּרְגּוּמוֹ וּמְכִילָתֵיהּ, הֵן סְנִיפִים כְּמִין יִתְדוֹת זָהָב
sources.says: Rashi says, following the Aramaic, that they were props like gold pegs.

sources.quote: ומנקיתיו שהיו מנקין בהן את התנור מן הדשן
sources.says: Chizkuni says they were used to clean the ash out of the oven.

37:19.headline: Meshukadim: shaped like almonds, or engraved with designs?
37:19.body: שקד is an almond. Rashbam says the cups had almond-like bumps, and Ibn Ezra reports the same from Saadia Gaon. Rashi follows the Aramaic translation: they were engraved with designs. Ibn Ezra himself ties it to שקד, 'to keep watch'.

sources.quote: משקדים - כעין שקדים
sources.says: Rashbam says they were like almonds, raised shapes on the walls of the cups.

sources.quote: משקדים. כְּתַרְגּוּמוֹ, מְצֻיָּרִים הָיוּ
sources.says: Rashi says, following the Aramaic, that they were engraved with designs.

sources.quote: אמר הגאון כי משקדים כדמות שקדים, והנכון שהוא מגזרת לשקוד על דלתותי
sources.says: Ibn Ezra reports that the Gaon read it as almond-shaped, but says it comes from 'to watch daily at my doors'.

37:20.headline: A word in the Torah that could belong to either side
37:20.body: משקדים sits between 'four cups' and 'its knobs and flowers'. Rashi, citing the Talmud, says it is one of five verses with no way to decide: it may describe the cups before it, or the knobs and flowers after it.

sources.quote: זֶה אֶחָד מֵחֲמִשָּׁה מִקְרָאוֹת שֶׁאֵין לָהֶם הֶכְרֵעַ (יומא נ"ב), אֵין יָדוּעַ אִם גְּבִיעִים מְשֻׁקָּדִים אוֹ מְשֻׁקָּדִים כַּפְתּוֹרֶיהָ וּפְרָחֶיהָ
sources.says: Rashi says this is one of five verses that cannot be decided: it is not known whether the cups are meshukadim or the knobs and flowers are.

sources.quote: חָמֵשׁ מִקְרָאוֹת בַּתּוֹרָה אֵין לָהֶן הֶכְרֵעַ
sources.says: The Talmud says there are five verses in the Torah whose reading cannot be decided.

sources.quote: שְׂאֵת״. ״מְשׁוּקָּדִים״. ״מָחָר״. ״אָרוּר״. ״וְקָם
sources.says: The Talmud lists the five, and משוקדים is the second of them.

38:8.headline: Moses did not want the women's mirrors; God said they were dearest
38:8.body: Rashi says Moses wanted to refuse the women's copper mirrors as tools of vanity, but God told him to accept them, for they were dearer to Him than anything. Chizkuni adds a reading from 'seeing': the basin stood where the women would see it and remember that its water tested a suspected wife.

sources.quote: וְהָיָה מוֹאֵס מֹשֶׁה בָּהֶן מִפְּנֵי שֶׁעֲשׂוּיִם לְיֵצֶר הָרָע, אָמַר לוֹ הַקָּבָּ"ה קַבֵּל, כִּי אֵלּוּ חֲבִיבִין עָלַי מִן הַכֹּל
sources.says: Rashi says Moses rejected them because they were made for the evil inclination, and God told him: accept, for these are dearer to Me than everything.

sources.quote: במראת הצבאת לשון ראיה פי׳‎ היה נתון בין אהל מועד ובין המזבח משוך מעט כלפי צפון כדי שתראנה אותו הנשים הצובאות ויהיה נזכר להם שמשם משקים את הסוטות
sources.says: Chizkuni reads מראות as 'seeing': the basin stood where the gathering women would see it and remember that the suspected wife is given its water to drink.

38:8.headline: 'The women who gathered': mothers of hosts, or women at prayer?
38:8.body: Rashi links הצבאת to צבאות, hosts: with these mirrors the women had raised many children in Egypt. Ibn Ezra says they were women who had given up vanity and came in crowds to the Tent each day to pray and hear the commandments.

sources.quote: שֶׁעַל יְדֵיהֶם הֶעֱמִידוּ הַנָּשִׁים צְבָאוֹת רַבּוֹת בְּמִצְרַיִם
sources.says: Rashi says through these mirrors the women raised up many hosts in Egypt.

sources.quote: והנה היו בישראל נשים עובדות השם שסרו מתאות זה העולם, ונתנו מראותיהן נדבה, כי אין להם צורך עוד להתיפות, רק באות יום יום אל פתח האהל מועד להתפלל ולשמוע דברי המצות
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says there were women in Israel who served God and turned from worldly desire; they gave their mirrors, having no more need to beautify themselves, and came daily to the Tent's door to pray and hear the commandments.

38:14.headline: The courtyard has 'shoulders', as if it were a person facing east
38:14.body: Ibn Ezra says the Tent's door faces east like a face. So the back side is called 'thighs', and the sides next to the entrance are called כתף, shoulders, like a man's.

sources.quote: ובעבור שפתח אוהל מועד למזרח כמו הפנים על כן קרא לפאת ים ירכים וקרא הקרובים אל הפתח כתפים ככתפות איש
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says since the Tent's door is east like a face, the west side is called thighs and the parts near the door are called shoulders, like a man's shoulders.

38:21.headline: 'Mishkan' twice: a sanctuary that would be taken in pledge
38:21.body: Rashi says משכן appears twice to hint at משכון, a pledge: the Temple would be 'taken in pledge' in two destructions for Israel's sins. Bahya also hears המשכה, drawing: the sanctuary below draws its power from the one above.

sources.quote: המשכן משכן. שְׁנֵי פְעָמִים, רֶמֶז לַמִּקְדָשׁ שֶׁנִּתְמַשְׁכֵּן בִּשְׁנֵי חֻרְבָּנִין עַל עֲוֹנוֹתֵיהֶן שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל
sources.says: Rashi says 'Mishkan' twice hints at the Temple, which was taken as a pledge in two destructions for Israel's sins.

sources.quote: וגם יתכן שנבין מלת משכן מלשון המשכה לפי שהמשכן וכליו ציורים ודוגמא למקדש של מעלה
sources.says: Bahya says the word משכן may also come from 'drawing', since the Tabernacle and its vessels are images of the sanctuary above.

38:21.headline: 'Tabernacle of testimony': it held the tablets, and proved forgiveness
38:21.body: Ibn Ezra and Chizkuni say it is called the Tabernacle of העדות because the tablets of testimony rested in it. Rashi reads it as testimony to Israel that God forgave the golden calf, since He brought His presence to live among them.

sources.quote: ופירש למה נקרא משכן, בעבור הארון ששם לוחות העדות
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the verse explains why it is called the Tabernacle: because of the ark, where the tablets of testimony were.

sources.quote: אומר לך כאן שהוא משכן העדת שהלוחות שוכנות בו
sources.says: Chizkuni says it is the Tabernacle of testimony, in which the tablets rest.

sources.quote: משכן העדת. עֵדוּת לְיִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁוִּתֵּר לָהֶם הַקָּבָּ"ה עַל מַעֲשֵׂה הָעֵגֶל, שֶׁהֲרֵי הִשְׁרָה שְׁכִינָתוֹ בֵּינֵיהֶם
sources.says: Rashi says it is testimony to Israel that God forgave them for the golden calf, since He rested His presence among them.

38:22.headline: Bezalel stood 'in God's shadow' and guessed God's plan
38:22.body: Moses told Bezalel to make the furniture first and the building after. Bezalel said people build a house first and then fill it, and Moses answered: you were בצל אל, in God's shadow, for that is what God told me.

sources.quote: אָמַר לוֹ בְּצַלְאֵל מִנְהַג עוֹלָם לַעֲשׂוֹת תְּחִלָּה בַּיִת וְאַחַר כָּךְ מֵשִׂים כֵּלִים בְּתוֹכוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says Bezalel told Moses the way of the world is to make the house first and then put the furniture in it.

sources.quote: אָמַר לוֹ מֹשֶׁה בְּצֵל אֵל הָיִיתָ, כִּי בְּוַדַּאי כָּךְ צִוָּה לִי הקב"ה
sources.says: Rashi says Moses answered: you were in the shadow of God, for that is surely what God commanded me.

39:1.headline: בגדי שרד: cloths of service, or cloths of open needlework?
39:1.body: Rashi says these are not the priests' clothes, since no linen is listed: they are the cloths that covered the holy vessels on the march. Onkelos reads שרד as 'service'. Rashi takes it from Aramaic: cloth worked with a needle, full of small holes.

sources.quote: שֵׁשׁ לֹא נֶאֱמַר כָּאן, וּמִכָּאן אֲנִי אוֹמֵר שֶׁאֵין בִּגְדֵי שְׂרָד הַלָּלוּ בִּגְדֵי כְהֻנָּה
sources.says: Rashi says linen is not mentioned here, so these are not the priests' garments.

sources.quote: יֵשׁ מְפָרְשִׁים לְשׁוֹן עֲבוֹדָה וְשֵׁרוּת, כְּתַרְגּוּמוֹ לְבוּשֵׁי שִׁמּוּשָׁא, וְאֵין לוֹ דִּמְיוֹן בַּמִּקְרָא
sources.says: Rashi reports that some read שרד as service, as Onkelos does, though it has no parallel in Scripture.

sources.quote: וַאֲנִי אוֹמֵר שֶׁהוּא לְשׁוֹן אֲרַמִּי
sources.says: Rashi says he takes it as Aramaic, for cloth worked with a needle, full of holes.

39:3.headline: The one place the Torah explains how the craftsmen worked
39:3.body: Rashi says they hammered gold into thin sheets and cut threads from them, like God 'spreading out' (רקע) the earth. Ramban notes this is the only place in the whole building account that describes a method. He suggests why: spinning gold into thread like wool or linen was something new.

sources.quote: טַסִּין הָיוּ מְרַדְּדִין מִן הַזָּהָב
sources.says: Rashi says they beat the gold into thin plates.

sources.quote: לֹא הוֹסִיף בְּכָל מְלֶאכֶת הַקֹּדֶשׁ לְפָרֵשׁ דֶּרֶךְ הָאֻמָּנוּת אֵיךְ נַעֲשָׂה, זוּלָתִי בְּכָאן
sources.says: Ramban says nowhere else in the holy work does the Torah explain how the craft was done.

sources.quote: ויתכן שספר כאן המחשבה שחדשו בחוטי הזהב כי היה תמה בעיניהם להיות זהב טווי ושזור
sources.says: Bahya, quoting Ramban, says the verse tells of the new idea of gold thread, since spun and twisted gold amazed them.

39:25.headline: Bells between the pomegranates, or hidden inside them?
39:25.body: Rashi reads בתוך as 'between': a gold bell hung between each pair of pomegranates. Ramban reads it as 'inside': the pomegranates were hollow and the bells sat within them. He says this verse shows it, since they put the bells in before sewing the pomegranates on.

sources.quote: בֵּינֵיהֶם סָבִיב – בֵּין שְׁנֵי רִמּוֹנִים פַּעֲמוֹן אֶחָד
sources.says: Rashi says it means among them: one bell between every two pomegranates.

sources.quote: אֲבָל הֵם בְּתוֹכָם מַמָּשׁ, כִּי הָרִמּוֹנִים חֲלוּלִים
sources.says: Ramban says the bells were really inside them, since the pomegranates were hollow.

sources.quote: וַיָּשִׂימוּ הַפַּעֲמוֹנִים בְּתוֹךְ הָרִמּוֹנִים קֹדֶם שֶׁיִּתְּנוּ אוֹתָם בַּמְּעִיל
sources.says: Ramban says they placed the bells inside the pomegranates before attaching them to the robe.

39:37.headline: Why the menorah is called 'the pure one'
39:37.body: Chizkuni says it is called pure because no blood was ever sprinkled on it. Bekhor Shor says it was the only vessel made wholly of gold, with no wood inside.

sources.quote: את המנרה הטהרה על שם שלא היה מזין עליה שום דם
sources.says: Chizkuni says it is called pure because no blood was sprinkled on it.

sources.quote: לא היה שם כלי כולו של זהב שלא היה בו עץ חוץ מן המנורה
sources.says: Bekhor Shor says no vessel there was all gold without wood except the menorah.

39:11.headline: נפך: Judah's stone, which makes enemies turn their backs
39:11.body: Rabbeinu Bahya says the נפך was Judah's stone. Whoever wears it, he says, sees his enemies turn their backs, הופכין, and that is why it is called נפך, as Jacob blessed Judah: 'your hand on your enemies' neck'.

sources.quote: וסגולת האבן הזאת שכל מי שנושאם אויביו הופכין לו עורף ולכך נקרא נפך
sources.says: Bahya says whoever carries this stone sees his enemies turn their backs, and so it is called נפך.

39:12.headline: אחלמה: Gad's stone, named for strength
39:12.body: Rabbeinu Bahya says the אחלמה was Gad's stone. It strengthens the heart so a man does not lose courage in war, and it is named from חלם, 'strong', as in Hezekiah's 'You made me strong and gave me life'.

sources.quote: וסגולת האבן הזאת שמחזקת את הלב שלא ירך בלכתו למלחמה ולכך נקראת אחלמה מלשון חוזק
sources.says: Bahya says this stone strengthens the heart so one does not weaken going to war, so it is named אחלמה, from strength.

39:13.headline: ישפה, Benjamin's stone: 'there is a mouth', yet he kept silent
39:13.body: Rabbeinu Bahya reads ישפה as two words, יש פה, 'there is a mouth'. Benjamin wrestled over whether to tell his father about Joseph's sale, and he held his tongue.

sources.quote: ונקראת ישפה שתי מלות יש פה, וזה יורה על מעלתו שאע"פ שהיה לו פה והיה לו לגלות הדבר שתק ולא גלה
sources.says: Bahya says ישפה is two words, יש פה: though Benjamin had a mouth and could have revealed the matter, he kept silent.

4:2.headline: Written as one word: 'from this' you deserve a beating
4:2.body: The text is read מה זה, 'what is this', but written as one word, מזה, 'from this'. Rashi says the spelling hints that Moses deserved to be struck with that staff for doubting innocent people. Plainly, God first has Moses agree it is a staff, then changes it.

sources.quote: לְכָךְ נִכְתַּב תֵּבָה אַחַת, לִדְרֹשׁ: מִזֶּה שֶׁבְּיָדְךָ אַתָּה חַיָּב לִלְקוֹת, שֶׁחָשַׁדְתָּ בִכְשֵׁרִים
sources.says: Rashi says it is written as one word to teach: with this in your hand you deserve to be struck, because you suspected decent people.

sources.quote: כְּאָדָם שֶׁאוֹמֵר לַחֲבֵרוֹ מוֹדֶה אַתָּה שֶׁזּוֹ שֶׁלְּפָנֶיךָ אֶבֶן הִיא
sources.says: Rashi gives the plain sense: like a man who gets his friend to agree something is a stone before turning it into wood.

4:3.headline: A snake, because Moses had spoken badly of Israel
4:3.body: Rashi asks why the sign was a snake. He says it hinted that Moses had spoken ill of Israel, which is the snake's trade. Ramban adds that this is why Moses ran from it: he feared the snake would bite him as punishment.

sources.quote: רָמַז לוֹ שֶׁסִּפֵּר לָשׁוֹן הָרָע עַל יִשְׂרָאֵל וְתָפַשׂ אֻמָּנוּתוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ
sources.says: Rashi says the snake hinted that Moses spoke ill of Israel and so took up the snake's trade.

sources.quote: וְזֶה טַעַם וַיָּנָס מֹשֶׁה מִפָּנָיו, כִּי פָּחַד שֶׁמָּא יֵעָנֵשׁ וִינַשְּׁכוֹ הַנָּחָשׁ
sources.says: Ramban says Moses fled because he feared he would be punished and the snake would bite him.

4:6.headline: A skin disease for speaking ill, as Miriam later got
4:6.body: Rashi reads the white, diseased hand as a second hint: Moses had spoken ill of Israel when he said 'they will not believe me'. So he was struck the way Miriam was struck for speaking ill. Rabbeinu Bahya also sees a lesson in the pair of signs: a dead stick came alive, and a living hand became like dead.

sources.quote: אַף בְּאוֹת זֶה רָמַז לוֹ שֶׁלָּשׁוֹן הָרָע סִפֵּר בְּאָמְרוֹ לֹא יַאֲמִינוּ לִי, לְפִיכָךְ הִלְקָהוּ בְצָרַעַת
sources.says: Rashi says this sign too hinted that Moses spoke ill in saying 'they will not believe me', so God struck him with this skin disease.

sources.quote: כי המטה היה עץ יבש כמו מת ונעשה נחש חי גם ידו שהיתה חיה נעשית כמתה
sources.says: Rabbeinu Bahya says the staff was dry wood, like something dead, and became a living snake, while the living hand became like dead.

4:9.headline: Why 'they shall become' twice in one sentence?
4:9.body: The verse says והיו, 'they shall become', twice. Rashi reads the second one as a detail: the Nile water turns to blood only once it is on the dry ground, not in Moses' hand. Ramban disagrees: Hebrew often repeats a word just for force.

sources.quote: אֲבָל עַכְשָׁו מְלַמְּדֵנוּ שֶׁלֹּא יִהְיוּ דָם עַד שֶׁיִּהְיוּ בַיַּבָּשֶׁת
sources.says: Rashi says the doubled word teaches that the water will not become blood until it is on the dry ground.

sources.quote: שֶׁדֶּרֶךְ הַרְבֵּה מִקְרָאוֹת לִכְפֹּל תֵּבוֹת לְנַחֵץ וּלְחַזֵּק
sources.says: Ramban says many verses repeat words simply to press and strengthen the point.

4:10.headline: בי: 'please', or 'let the blame fall on me'
4:10.body: בי looks like 'in me'. Ibn Ezra says the commentators all read it as a word of pleading. Rabbi Yehuda Halevi reads it as short for 'on me be it': punish me as you like, only do not send me.

sources.quote: כל המפרשים פה אחד אמרו, כי פרוש בי לשון בקשה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says all the commentators agree that בי is a word of request.

sources.quote: כלומר עשה בי עונש מה שתרצה, והניחני מזה שלא תשלחני
sources.says: Ibn Ezra reports Rabbi Yehuda Halevi's reading: do to me whatever punishment you wish, but spare me from being sent.

4:10.headline: Seven days at the bush: Moses kept saying no
4:10.body: Rashi counts the words: 'yesterday', 'the day before', 'since you spoke', and three times גם, 'also'. That makes six days, and Moses is still refusing on the seventh. Rashi says he held back so as not to rise above his older brother Aaron.

sources.quote: לָמַדְנוּ שֶׁכָּל ז' יָמִים הָיָה הַקָּבָּ"ה מְפַתֶּה אֶת מֹשֶׁה בַּסְּנֶה לֵילֵךְ בִּשְׁלִיחוּתוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says that for seven days God urged Moses at the bush to go on his mission.

sources.quote: וְכָל זֶה שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה רוֹצֶה לִטֹּל גְּדֻלָּה עַל אַהֲרֹן אָחִיו
sources.says: Rashi says Moses refused because he did not want to take greatness over his brother Aaron.

4:10.headline: Heavy of mouth: a speech problem, or rusty Egyptian?
4:10.body: Rashi says Moses spoke with difficulty. Ibn Ezra says he was born unable to say some sounds easily. Rashbam rejects the idea that so great a prophet stammered: Moses had fled Egypt as a boy and no longer spoke its language well.

sources.quote: כבד פה. בִּכְבֵדוּת אֲנִי מְדַבֵּר
sources.says: Rashi says it means: I speak with heaviness.

sources.quote: רק ככה נולד שהיה כבד פה שלא היה יכול להוציא אותיות השפה וכל אותיות הלשון
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says Moses was born this way and had trouble saying letters made with the lips and tongue.

sources.quote: איני בקי בלשון מצרים בחיתוך לשון, כי בקטנותי ברחתי משם ועתה אני בן שמונים
sources.says: Rashbam says Moses meant he was not fluent in Egyptian, having fled as a child and now being eighty.

4:11.headline: How can God 'make' someone mute, if muteness is only a lack?
4:11.body: Muteness is not a thing but the lack of speech, so how is it 'set'? Maimonides answers that whoever takes away a power is said to make its lack, as one who puts out a lamp 'makes' the dark. Or the verse means God creates a person without the power of speech.

sources.quote: כך אנו אומרים על מי שהשחית את הראייה שהוא עשה את העיוורון
sources.says: Maimonides says that just as one who puts out a lamp is said to cause darkness, one who destroys sight is said to make blindness.

sources.quote: מי הוא אשר ברא את האדם בעל יכולת דיבור, או בורא אותו בלא יכולת לדבר
sources.says: Maimonides offers a second reading: who creates a person able to speak, or creates him without that ability.

sources.quote: כִּי הָאִלְּמוּת לֹא יוּשַׁם, כִּי אֵינֶנּוּ דָּבָר, אֲבָל הוּא הֶעְדֵּר הַדִּבּוּר
sources.says: Ramban notes the problem: muteness cannot be set in place, since it is not a thing but the absence of speech.

4:11.headline: Who made Pharaoh mute and his guards blind when you fled?
4:11.body: Rashi reads God's question as a reminder of Moses' own escape. God made Pharaoh mute, so he did not press the order to kill Moses. He made the servants deaf to the order and the executioners blind as Moses ran.

sources.quote: מִי עָשָׂה פַרְעֹה אִלֵּם, שֶׁלֹּא נִתְאַמֵּץ בְּמִצְוַת הֲרִיגָתְךָ
sources.says: Rashi says God made Pharaoh mute, so that he did not insist on the order to kill Moses.

sources.quote: וְאֶת אֶסְפַּקְלָטוֹרִין הַהוֹרְגִים מִי עֲשָׂאָם עִוְרִים שֶׁלֹּא רָאוּ כְּשֶׁבָּרַחְתָּ
sources.says: Rashi says God made the executioners blind so they did not see Moses run away.

4:11.headline: One word for open eyes and open ears
4:11.body: פקח, open, is used of eyes and of ears. That is why it stands between 'deaf' and 'blind': it is the opposite of both. Ibn Ezra and Chizkuni both point to Isaiah, who opens ears and opens blind eyes.

sources.quote: והאמת כי מלת פקח כנגד החרש והעור, ככתוב פקוח אזנים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says פקח is the opposite of both deaf and blind, as Isaiah speaks of opening ears and opening eyes.

sources.quote: פקח הטילו הכתוב בין חרש לעור לפי שהוא נופל על שניהם
sources.says: Chizkuni says the verse put פקח between deaf and blind because it applies to both.

4:13.headline: 'Send by the hand you will send': but whose hand?
4:13.body: Moses does not say who. Rashi gives two readings: the one you usually send, Aaron; or anyone else, since I am not the one who will bring them into the land. Onkelos reads: whoever is fit to be sent.

sources.quote: בְּיַד מִי שֶׁאַתָּה רָגִיל לִשְׁלֹחַ, וְהוּא אַהֲרֹן
sources.says: Rashi says it means by the hand of the one you usually send, which is Aaron.

sources.quote: בְּיַד אַחֵר שֶׁתִּרְצֶה לִשְׁלֹחַ, אֵין סוֹפִי לְהַכְנִיסָם לָאָרֶץ
sources.says: Rashi's second reading: by anyone else you wish, since Moses is not destined to bring them into the land.

sources.quote: בְּיַד מָן דְכָשַׁר דְתִשְׁלַח
sources.says: Onkelos translates: by the hand of whoever is fit for you to send.

4:14.headline: 'Aaron the Levite': the priesthood passes from Moses to Aaron
4:14.body: Moses was a Levite too, so why call Aaron 'the Levite'? Rashi says God's anger left a mark here. The priesthood was meant for Moses, with Aaron staying a plain Levite. Now it went to Aaron.

sources.quote: שֶׁהָיָה עָתִיד לִהְיוֹת לֵוִי וְלֹא כֹּהֵן, וְהַכְּהֻנָּה הָיִיתִי אוֹמֵר לָצֵאת מִמְּךָ
sources.says: Rashi says Aaron was meant to be a Levite and not a priest, and the priesthood was to come from Moses.

sources.quote: מֵעַתָּה לֹא יִהְיֶה כֵן אֶלָּא הוּא יִהְיֶה כֹּהֵן וְאַתָּה הַלֵּוִי
sources.says: Rashi says that from now on it would be reversed: Aaron the priest and Moses the Levite.

4:14.headline: Glad in his heart, so his heart wore the breastplate
4:14.body: The verse says Aaron will be glad 'in his heart', not just outwardly. Rashi says Aaron would not resent his younger brother's rise. For this he earned the priest's breastplate, worn over the heart.

sources.quote: לֹא כְשֶׁאַתָּה סָבוּר, שֶׁיְּהֵא מַקְפִּיד עָלֶיךָ שֶׁאַתָּה עוֹלֶה לִגְדֻלָּה
sources.says: Rashi says Aaron will not resent Moses for rising to greatness, as Moses fears.

sources.quote: וּמִשָּׁם זָכָה אַהֲרֹן לַעֲדִי הַחֹשֶׁן הַנָּתוּן עַל הַלֵּב
sources.says: Rashi says that for this Aaron earned the breastplate placed over the heart.

sources.quote: ושמח בפיו לא נאמר אלא בלבו
sources.says: Rabbeinu Bahya points out the verse says glad in his heart, not glad in his mouth.

4:19.headline: 'The men are dead': or only poor
4:19.body: Rashi says the men who wanted Moses dead were Dathan and Abiram. They were still alive, but they had lost their wealth, and a poor man counts as dead. Ibn Ezra reads it plainly: Pharaoh and his servants had died.

sources.quote: דָּתָן וַאֲבִירָם; חַיִּים הָיוּ, אֶלָּא שֶׁיָּרְדוּ מִנִּכְסֵיהֶם וְהֶעָנִי חָשׁוּב כַּמֵּת
sources.says: Rashi says it was Dathan and Abiram, who were alive but had lost their property, and a poor man is counted as dead.

sources.quote: כי מת פרעה ועבדיו שהיו יודעים דבר המצרי
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says Pharaoh and the servants who knew about the Egyptian Moses killed had died.

4:20.headline: Not a donkey but 'the' donkey
4:20.body: The verse says החמר, 'the donkey', as if a known one. Rashi, from a midrash, says it was the donkey Abraham saddled for the binding of Isaac, the one the Messiah will ride. Ibn Ezra brings a plainer view: 'the donkey' just names the kind of animal.

sources.quote: חֲמוֹר הַמְיֻחָד, הוּא הַחֲמוֹר שֶׁחָבַשׁ אַבְרָהָם לַעֲקֵדַת יִצְחָק
sources.says: Rashi says it was the special donkey, the one Abraham saddled for the binding of Isaac.

sources.quote: ויפת אמר כי הוא שם המין
sources.says: Ibn Ezra cites Yefet that 'the donkey' is just the name of the species.

4:22.headline: 'My firstborn' means my great one
4:22.body: Rashi says בכרי, my firstborn, is a word of greatness, as in Psalms: 'I will make him my firstborn'. His midrashic reading: here God signed off on the firstborn rights Jacob bought from Esau.

sources.quote: בני בכרי. לְשׁוֹן גְּדֻלָּה; כְּמוֹ: "אַף אֲנִי בְּכוֹר אֶתְּנֵהוּ"
sources.says: Rashi says 'my firstborn' is a term of greatness, as in Psalms: 'I too will make him my firstborn'.

sources.quote: כָּאן חָתַם הַקָּבָּ"ה עַל מְכִירַת הַבְּכוֹרָה שֶׁלָּקַח יַעֲקֹב מֵעֵשָׂו
sources.says: Rashi's midrash: here God sealed the sale of the birthright Jacob took from Esau.

4:25.headline: חתן: her husband, or the baby being circumcised
4:25.body: Rashi reads Zipporah as speaking to her son: because of you my husband (חתן) is being killed. Ibn Ezra notes that women used to call a boy at his circumcision a חתן, a bridegroom.

sources.quote: אַתָּה הָיִיתָה גּוֹרֵם לִהְיוֹת הֶחָתָן שֶׁלִּי נִרְצָח עָלֶיךָ
sources.says: Rashi says she told her son: you caused my bridegroom to be killed on your account.

sources.quote: ומנהג הנשים לקרוא לבן כאשר יומל חתן
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says women were used to calling a boy a חתן when he was circumcised.

4:26.headline: Blood that kills, or blood of the covenant
4:26.body: Ibn Ezra says דמים has two senses: bloodshed, and actual drops of blood. When the danger passed, Zipporah changed her meaning: not a groom of killing, but a groom covered in the blood of circumcision.

sources.quote: דמים בלשון הקדש על ב' ענינים, האחד שפיכות דמים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says דמים has two meanings in Hebrew, the first being bloodshed.

sources.quote: רק אתה חתן מתבוסס בדם המילה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says she meant: you are a groom wallowing in the blood of circumcision.

5:3.headline: Three ways to explain the name "Hebrews"
5:3.body: Moses calls God אלהי העברים, "the God of the Hebrews". Ibn Ezra ties the name to Abraham, who was called the Hebrew, Rashbam to people who came from across the river, and Sforno to people who keep the beliefs of Ever.

sources.quote: זה השם הוא אלהי העברים שהיו יודעים והוא אברהם הנקרא עברי
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says this is the God the Hebrews knew, starting with Abraham, who was called the Hebrew.

sources.quote: עם ישראל מעבר הנהר באו לגור הנה וזהו אלהי בני עבר הנהר
sources.says: Rashbam says Israel came from across the river to live in Egypt, so this is the God of the people from across the river.

sources.quote: הַמְפֹרָסְמִים הַמַּחֲזִיקִים בְּדֵעוֹת עֵבֶר
sources.says: Sforno says the Hebrews are the well-known people who hold to the beliefs of Ever.

5:3.headline: "May strike us" was a polite way to warn Pharaoh
5:3.body: Moses warns that a plague "may strike us". Rashi says they meant "strike you" but spoke politely to a king, and Ibn Ezra says "us" took in Israel and Egypt together.

sources.quote: פֶּן יִפְגָּעֲךָ הָיוּ צְרִיכִים לוֹמַר, אֶלָּא שֶׁחָלְקוּ כָּבוֹד לַמַּלְכוּת
sources.says: Rashi says they should have said "lest He strike you" but showed respect to the king.

sources.quote: מלת פן יפגענו, כוללת אנחנו ישראלים, גם אתה פרעה עמנו וכל המצריים
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the word "us" includes the Israelites and also Pharaoh and all the Egyptians.

5:9.headline: Talk about lies, pay attention to lies, or go slack?
5:9.body: ישעו can be read three ways. Rashi reads "let them not chatter about false words", Rashbam reads "let them not pay attention to them", and Ibn Ezra reads "let them not go slack because of them".

sources.quote: אַל יִהְיוּ נִדְבָּרִים בְּדִבְרֵי שָׁוְא וַהֲבַאי
sources.says: Rashi says it means they should not keep talking about empty words, and he rejects reading it as "turn toward".

sources.quote: כמו: וישע אל הבל. ולא ישעה אל המזבחות
sources.says: Rashbam reads it as "pay attention", like God paying regard to Abel.

sources.quote: ולפי דעתי כי ישעו כמו ירפו, כאשר אמר "נרפים"
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says ישעו means "slacken", matching Pharaoh's word נרפים, "lazy".

5:21.headline: A bad smell "in the eyes" of Pharaoh
5:21.body: The officers say Moses made "our smell stink in Pharaoh's eyes", which mixes smell and sight. Ibn Ezra says the senses meet in one place in the head, so Scripture can name one sense in place of another.

sources.quote: ודע כי החמש הרגשות מתחברות במקום אחד למעלה מהמצח על כן יאמרו הרגשה אחת תחת חברתה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the five senses join in one place above the forehead, so one sense is named in place of another.

5:22.headline: Moses calls God "Lord", not the name of mercy
5:22.body: Here Moses says אדני, written with the letters alef and dalet. Ramban says he did not use the four-letter name, which stands for mercy, because mercy does not bring harm on a people.

sources.quote: נִכְתַּב בְּאָלֶ"ף דָּלֶ"ת, כִּי הַשֵּׁם הַמְּיֻחָד שֶׁהוּא מִדַּת הָרַחֲמִים לֹא יָרֵעַ לָעָם
sources.says: Ramban says the name is written alef-dalet because the special name, the attribute of mercy, does not harm the people.

sources.quote: כי ממדת רחמים לא היה משה מפחד שיריע לעם
sources.says: Rabbeinu Bahya says Moses did not fear that mercy would harm the people; he feared strict judgment.

5:22.headline: A complaint against God, or an honest question?
5:22.body: Moses asks God למה הרעתה, "why have You done harm?" Rabbeinu Bahya cites Rabbeinu Chananel that this is a question, not a protest: why did You let harm come when You could save them?

sources.quote: שאין לשון למה הרעותה לשון תלונה והטחת דברים אבל הוא לשון שאלה
sources.says: Rabbeinu Bahya cites Rabbeinu Chananel that "why have You done harm" is not a complaint but a question.

sources.quote: שאל להש"י למה הנחת להרע לעם הזה ובידך כח להצילם
sources.says: He says Moses asked why God let harm come to the people when He had the power to save them.

6:3.headline: "I was not known", not "I did not tell them"
6:3.body: The fathers did know the name יהוה, so the verse seems odd. Rashi points to the verb form: it says God was not known by them, not that he never told them. They had not yet seen him keep his promises, which is what this name stands for.

sources.quote: לֹא הוֹדַעְתִּי אֵין כְּתִיב כָּאן אֶלָּא לֹא נוֹדַעְתִּי, לֹא נִכַּרְתִּי לָהֶם בְּמִדַת אֲמִתּוּת שֶׁלִּי, שֶׁעָלֶיהָ נִקְרָא שְׁמִי ה', נֶאֱמָן לְאַמֵּת דְּבָרַי, שֶׁהֲרֵי הִבְטַחְתִּים וְלֹא קִיַּמְתִּי
